_meta.why: The plaque is person-keyed and several people report their year on it is wrong. Years are the stable spine; people are attached to years and can be moved.

role_values.president: Led the student government that year
role_values.regent: Held the student seat on the WKU Board of Regents - a separately elected office from 1968 until the two merged
role_values.unresolved: Shares a year with another name and the split is not yet established

_meta.student_regent_history: The student regent seat was created by state legislation reported in committee in February 1968 and filled in April 1968 by William Menser. It carried no vote for at least four years - students were campaigning for voting power in February 1970 and the Herald was still reporting 'Student Regent May Get Vote' in February 1972. Because it was separately elected, several plaque years carry two names: one president and one regent.
_meta.dating: Events are filed under the academic year they belong to, August through July. One deliberate exception: a spring election is filed under the term it created, so the April 2026 election appears under 2026-27, the year it elected. Entries dated 1 January are items the archive can place in a year but not to a day; the date is a placeholder, not a claim.

leaders.name: Jim Haynes
leaders.note: First president of the Associated Students of Western Kentucky University, elected 18 May 1966, seven weeks after President Kelly Thompson approved the constitution.
profile: Jim Haynes was one of three candidates, with Leonard Heydt and John Lovett, who presented their views to the Herald in the race for the first presidency of the Associated Students in May 1966, days after the student body ratified the new constitution.

Haynes captured the presidency the following week, becoming the first president of the Associated Students of Western Kentucky University. The same issue carried a skeptical editorial titled 'We Do Not Deserve Student Government,' a measure of the doubts his administration set out to answer.
Haynes's term closed in May 1967, when the Herald summed up the government's first year as one of organization, progress and apathy and carried president-elect William Menser's plans for 1967-68.

events.title: President Kelly Thompson approves the constitution
events.body: The proposed constitution of the Associated Students of Western Kentucky University was completed in late March and approved on 1 April. The copy held by WKU Archives is dated 7 April 1966.

events.title: Thompson's approval letter is addressed to committee chair Reed Morgan
events.body: The archived copy of Thompson's approval letter names the organizing committee that drafted the constitution: Reed Morgan as chair, John Lovett as vice chair. Morgan's committee did the drafting; Jim Haynes was elected to lead the government it created six weeks later.

src.label: UA3/3/1, Letter to Organizational Committee for a Western Student Organization, 1 Apr 1966

events.title: Students ratify the constitution, 1,812 to 726
events.body: A four-day referendum. 2,538 students voted - a larger raw turnout than most SGA elections have managed since.

events.title: Jim Haynes elected first president
events.body: Seven weeks from presidential approval to a seated student president. Western Kentucky State College became Western Kentucky University on 16 June, so the university and its student government are almost exactly the same age.

events.title: The new government opens its first full year
events.body: The Herald's first issue of the fall reported the student senate ratifying a government appointment as the Associated Students began their first full academic year. Students had approved the constitution and elected officers the previous spring.

events.title: Doing well, but lacking communication
events.body: Midway through the fall semester the Herald judged that Associated Students leaders were performing well but were failing to communicate with the students they represented. It was the first public report card on the year-old government.

events.title: Two vie for the presidency
events.body: The Herald reported two candidates seeking the Associated Students presidency, with campaigns for the organization's second presidential election set to open the following Monday.

events.title: Swearing-in set for May 10
events.body: The Herald announced that newly elected Associated Student officers would be sworn in on May 10, 1967, completing the organization's first full transfer of leadership.

events.title: First year judged: organization, progress, apathy
events.body: Reviewing the government's first year, the Herald found organization and progress alongside persistent student apathy. The same issue carried president-elect William Menser's plans for 1967-68 and a letter arguing that the Associated Students really worked.

events.title: Dean Keown proposes a budget for the new government
events.body: Dean of Students Charles Keown sent President Kelly Thompson a memo proposing a student fee structure to create a budget for the Associated Student Government. He attached fee models gathered from universities across the South and Midwest.

events.title: Government and administration meet on campus problems
events.body: The Herald reported Student Government Association leaders meeting with President Kelly Thompson to discuss campus problems, an early instance of the year-old government dealing directly with the administration.

events.title: Herald warns of a 'popularity bandwagon' in the spring election
events.body: A week before the presidential campaign opened, the Herald ran a piece by Fran Salyers arguing that popularity, not merit, was set to decide the Associated Students election.

events.title: Herald presses students to vote as the year closes
events.body: Days after the outgoing administration's year-end review, the Herald ran a piece headlined 'Goof Government Needs Student Vote,' pressing students toward greater turnout as Menser's incoming administration took over.

events.title: A state association floated as the route to better entertainment
events.body: The first Herald of the Associated Students' first full year carried an article headed "Campus Entertainment Improvements Possible Through State Association," the earliest sign of the block-booking idea that would define the organisation's entertainment work for the next decade.

events.title: A monthly events calendar posted outside the Associated Students office
events.body: The Herald reported that the month's campus events were being posted outside the Associated Students office. It is the earliest standing service the record shows the new government running for students.

events.title: A student writes in wanting more entertainment
events.body: Tony Burdoc's letter, headed "Wants More Entertainment," ran in the Herald in April 1967, part of a running complaint about what the year-old government was putting on.

events.title: The case for a student book exchange
events.body: Mark Dossey reported in the Herald that student book exchanges were working at Murray State and the University of Louisville, an argument for Western to run one of its own. Through the rest of the decade the exchange on this campus was run by the Veterans Club, not by the Associated Students.

leaders.name: William Menser
leaders.note: ASG president 1967-68. On 4 April 1968 the Herald reported he 'assumes duties as Regent Board Member' - making him WKU's first student regent, two months after the enabling bill was reported in committee. The seat was non-voting at first.
profile: Menser headed the Associated Student Government from the start of the 1967-68 year, appearing alongside President Kelly Thompson in a 14 September 1967 Herald article welcoming students back to campus.

That fall the idea of a student seat on the Board of Regents was already circulating: a 2 November 1967 Herald article headlined 'Ward Favors Student on Board of Regents' reported support for the idea four months before an enabling bill reached committee.

That December the Herald reported an Associated Students survey of student activity preferences and, in the same 8 December 1967 issue, ran a piece by Dennis Jaffe commending the government's efforts; the same issue covered the Kentucky Intercollegiate Press Association backing a proposal for student representation.

In February 1968 Western sent lobbyists to Frankfort for a bill to seat a student on the Board of Regents; on 4 April 1968 the Herald reported Menser had assumed duties as the board's first student regent, a non-voting seat.

As his term closed, the Herald's 29 April 1968 issue - the same one covering the Straeffer-Whitley presidential race to succeed him - carried both a piece headlined 'Menser Discusses Head Fee' and a separate retrospective, 'Past Performance of Associated Student Government Analyzed'. The archive does not yet hold the text of either article, only their headlines.

Menser opened his year in office in September 1967 sharing the front page with President Kelly Thompson, in a piece headlined "Dr. Kelly Thompson, William Menser Welcome Students." The same first issue of the year set out the Associated Student Government's schedule of events.

Menser's correspondence with President Kelly Thompson survives in the WKU Archives, filed under student fees. The file is described as correspondence about the assessment of student fees and the Associated Student Government budget for 1968-1969.

events.title: Herald floats a student seat on the Board of Regents
events.body: A Herald article headlined 'Ward Favors Student on Board of Regents' reported support for putting a student on the Board of Regents, months before Western sent lobbyists to Frankfort or a bill reached committee.

events.title: ASG sponsors a Friday dance
events.body: The same issue that floated a student regent seat also reported the Associated Student Government sponsoring a campus dance that Friday.

events.title: WKU sends lobbyists to Frankfort for a student on the Board of Regents
events.body: The same Herald issue carries a tuition increase, a discussion group on major issues before the Associated Student Government and a committee investigating women's dormitory rules. This is the origin of the student regent seat.

events.title: A bill to put a student on the Board of Regents reaches committee
events.body: Reported by Ron Lawrence. Western had sent lobbyists to Frankfort for it earlier that month. The same issue carries students berating dorm rules and a letter headed 'Wanted: Work for Judicial Council'.

events.title: Herald questions ASG's Judicial Council as students organize a book swap
events.body: Bill Martin's column questioned the Judicial Council's work, while the same issue reported the Associated Student Government directing a student book swap.

events.title: Filing reveals few candidates for the spring election
events.body: Alana White reported that filing for Associated Student Government offices turned up few candidates, in the same issue as a piece urging that criteria for the offices be voiced.

events.title: William Menser becomes WKU's first student regent
events.body: Two months after the bill was in committee, the Herald reported that Menser 'assumes duties as Regent Board Member'. The seat carried no vote at first. The same issue opens candidate declarations for the next student government election.

events.title: Menser discusses the head fee
events.body: The same issue that opened coverage of the Straeffer-Whitley race to succeed him carried a piece on outgoing president Menser discussing the student head fee. The archive does not yet hold the article's text.

events.title: Herald analyzes ASG's past performance under Menser
events.body: A retrospective headlined 'Past Performance of Associated Student Government Analyzed' ran as Menser's term ended, in the same issue as the Straeffer-Whitley presidential campaign coverage. The archive does not yet hold the article's text.

events.title: Bill Straeffer wins the presidency; the Herald calls the election a failure
events.body: The issue reporting Straeffer's win also carries an editorial headed 'Elections Illustrate Faults, Indifference'. Turnout anxiety shows up in the second contested election the organisation ever held.

events.title: Menser and President Thompson open the school year together
events.body: The first Herald of the 1967-68 year carried a joint welcome to students headlined "Dr. Kelly Thompson, William Menser Welcome Students." The same issue ran an item headed "Associated Student Government Events Set," laying out the organisation's calendar for the coming term.

events.title: Associated Students discussion group takes up major campus issues
events.body: The Herald announced that major issues would be heard in an Associated Student Government discussion group. The same issue reported that Western had sent lobbyists in support of a bill to place a student on the Board of Regents, and carried coverage of a tuition increase.

events.title: Herald reviews the Associated Student Government's record
events.body: As Menser's term drew to a close the Herald ran an assessment headed "Past Performance of Associated Student Government Analyzed." It appeared in the same issue as the campaign coverage for the officers who would succeed him.

events.title: Rodes-Harlin Hall opens as a nine-story women's dorm
events.body: The Herald covered the opening of Rodes-Harlin Hall, a new nine-story women's residence hall, as campus construction continued to expand housing capacity.

events.title: The Associated Student Government sets its events for the year
events.body: The first Herald of 1967-68 announced the Associated Student Government's schedule of events for the coming year alongside the university's own lecture series and the Community Concerts season. It was the first year the government published a programme in advance.

events.title: Student government sets new programmes
events.body: The Herald reported that the student government had set new programmes for the year, in the same issue that announced Buckminster Fuller would lecture on campus and that Homecoming queen voting was set for Thursday.

events.title: The Four Tops booked for the Tuesday after the election
events.body: The Herald announced a Four Tops concert on campus the following Tuesday. The same issue reported the Associated Student Government sponsoring a dance that Friday and a Herald editorial arguing that campus groups needed more opportunity to run money-making events.

events.title: The Herald says the praise for student government is deserved
events.body: A Herald editorial headed "Praise for Associated Student Government Well Deserved" ran in November 1967, an unusually warm note in a paper that spent most of the era complaining about what the government booked.

events.title: Student government plans a push on campus activities
events.body: The Herald of 21 September 1967 carried Gary Hunt's report that student government was planning ahead to boost campus activities. The archive holds the issue as a contents listing, so the headline is all the record gives.

events.title: Herald reported Associated Students survey of activity preferences
events.body: The Herald published the results of an Associated Students survey of what activities students wanted, in a story by Ellen Bennett. The same issue carried a letter commending the Associated Student Government's efforts. It also reported the Kentucky Intercollegiate Press Association backing a proposal for student representation.

events.title: Kentucky Intercollegiate Press Association backed the student representation proposal
events.body: The Herald of 8 December 1967 reported that the Kentucky Intercollegiate Press Association had come out in support of the proposal for student representation. The item ran alongside the paper's coverage of Associated Students activity that week, including the Associated Students activity survey.

leaders.name: Reed Morgan
leaders.note: Single-year plate. Sits between Menser and Straeffer, whose election the Herald reported on 9 May 1968 - so Morgan likely finished a partial term or held the seat between elections. The only Reed Morgan found in the archive is a different, earlier role: chair of the organizing committee that received President Kelly Thompson's approval letter for the Associated Students constitution, 1 April 1966 - two years before this plaque entry. No Herald or WKU Timeline coverage connects a Reed Morgan to a 1968-69 SGA office. Left unresolved rather than moved, since the 1966 role (committee chair, pre-election) is not the same office the plaque implies. Re-checked 4 Aug 2026: fresh TopSCHOLAR searches (name plus SGA/regent/student-government terms) turned up only the same 1963-67 WKU Forensics team roster (M. Reed Morgan, debater) and the 1966 constitution-committee material already cited. Nothing new for 1968-69. The portrait on this page was published in the Herald of 7 April 1966, when Morgan was a graduating senior chairing the committee that drafted the constitution; it predates the plaque's 1968 placement by two years, and no source describes him as president.

sources.label: UA3/3/1, Letter to Organizational Committee for a Western Student Organization, 1 Apr 1966

profile: Reed Morgan chaired the student committee that drew up plans for a campus government in 1965-66. In March 1966, answering critics of the project's pace, Morgan replied in the Herald that the committee was not dragging its feet.

A month before students ratified the constitution, the Herald profiled Morgan as a senior who tripled as Greek editor, debater and government chairman, crediting him as a principal architect of the Associated Students plan. The digitized Herald index shows no student government coverage of Morgan in 1968-69 itself.

leaders.name: Bill Straeffer
leaders.note: Election win reported in the Herald, 9 May 1968, in the same issue as an editorial headed 'Elections Illustrate Faults, Indifference'. The internal election-results memo (mirrored below) gives his exact margin: 1,732 votes to Charles Whitley's 1,098.

sources.label: UA3/3/1 Memo Re: Results of Election, Ron Beck, 3 May 1968

profile: Straeffer ran for the Associated Students presidency against Charles Whitley in the 2 May 1968 election, the organization's second contested presidential race. He won 1,732 votes to Whitley's 1,098. Terry Gilpin was elected vice president in the same election, beating Bob Van Corbach 1,516 to 1,206. Total turnout was 2,894 votes, about 34 percent of the roughly 8,500-student enrollment - a turnout the Herald's coverage of the result treated as a persistent problem, running an editorial in the same issue headed 'Elections Illustrate Faults, Indifference'.

A year later, the Herald's 8 May 1969 issue carried Straeffer and Gilpin's own review of their year in office, headlined 'Associated Students Produces Year of Advancement,' alongside a companion piece, 'Bill Straeffer, Terry Gilpin Review Their Year with Associated Students.' The archive does not yet hold the article text itself, only its headline and byline (Ellen Bennett), so the specifics of what the administration counted as advancement are not yet confirmed.

Bill Straeffer vied with Charles Whitley for the Associated Student Government presidency in the spring 1968 election, the Herald carrying both hopefuls' ideas before the balloting, in a campaign that also saw Terry Gilpin and Bob Van Corbach contest the vice presidency.
Straeffer won the presidency in the May 1968 vote, and in the same issue the Herald reported the new president making plans for 1968-69.
Closing his term in May 1969, Straeffer and vice president Terry Gilpin reviewed their year with the Associated Students for the Herald, which credited the administration with a year of advancement.

leaders.name: Paul Gerard, III
leaders.note: Two-year plate reading 1968-70, immediately after William Menser took the first student regent seat in April 1968. Almost certainly the second student regent. Early student regents were non-voting 'associate regents', which may explain the longer term. Not yet confirmed as regent. A Paul Gerard did appear on the same 2 May 1968 ballot that elected Straeffer, winning the Junior Class presidency 461 votes to Mike Collins' 277 - circumstantially consistent (a junior in spring 1968 would be positioned for a campus-wide office the next year) but not proof of identity or of the regent seat specifically. Two people can share a name; this is flagged, not merged. Resolved: the 1969 Talisman captions him "Paul Gerard, the Student Regent" and the Herald of 27 February 1969 explains the mechanism - Kentucky's 1968 law required a student regent at every state campus, and because Associated Students president Bill Straeffer was an out-of-state student, the Congress of Associated Students elected Gerard, a Bowling Green junior and junior class president, to the seat instead. He sat as a non-voting member. Contemporary sources print his name without the suffix the plaque carries.

sources.label: UA3/3/1 Memo Re: Results of Election, Ron Beck, 3 May 1968

profile: Paul Gerard first appeared in the Herald's campus politics coverage in April 1968, when the paper reported him battling Mike Collins for a senior class post in that week's election.

By February 1969 Gerard held the student seat on the Board of Regents, and Herald writer Bruce Tucker profiled him as the student regent. He followed William Menser, who in April 1968 had become the first student to sit with the board.

events.title: Straeffer and Whitley vie for the presidency
events.body: The Herald's pre-election coverage set out the field: Bill Straeffer against Charles Whitley for president, Terry Gilpin against Bob Van Corbach for vice president, and contested races down to secretary, treasurer, and congressman at large.

events.title: Straeffer elected president, 1,732 to 1,098; turnout 34 percent
events.body: The Associated Students' internal election-results memo lists the full slate: Bill Straeffer over Charles Whitley for president, Terry Gilpin over Bob Van Corbach for vice president, Becky Cooper over Mary Miller for secretary, Tonii Rizzo over John Combs for treasurer, and John Cobelli and Janie Heathcoat elected congressmen at large over Billy Goodman and Scott Phillips. Total turnout was 2,894 votes, about 34 percent of enrollment.

src.label: UA3/3/1 Memo Re: Results of Election, Ron Beck, 3 May 1968

events.title: Straeffer and Gilpin review their year
events.body: The Herald ran the outgoing administration's own account of its year under the headline 'Associated Students Produces Year of Advancement,' alongside a companion piece on Straeffer and Gilpin reviewing their term.

events.title: Committees go to work
events.body: The Herald reported Associated Students committees swinging into action as the year began. The same issue noted that booking problems still plagued the group's entertainment calendar.

events.title: Judicial Council begins hearing cases
events.body: The Associated Students Judicial Council was hearing student cases, the Herald reported, an early exercise of the judicial power the young government claimed under its constitution.

events.title: Bringing speakers and shows to the Hill
events.body: The Herald reported the Associated Students working to bring speakers and entertainment to campus, alongside notice of an upcoming Associated Students dance.

events.title: A buffer against campus turmoil
events.body: As campus unrest spread nationally, the Herald suggested the Associated Student Government could deter turmoil at Western. The same issue reported president Bill Straeffer moving to discontinue the Greek-oriented Campus Favorites election.

events.title: Paul Gerard profiled as student regent
events.body: Herald writer Bruce Tucker profiled student regent Paul Gerard, and the paper reported a committee appointed to study revision of the Associated Students constitution.

events.title: Election Tuesday as declarations continue
events.body: Declarations of candidacy continued as the Associated Students election was set for the following Tuesday.

events.title: Zielke and Porter outline the coming year
events.body: Incoming leaders Larry Zielke and David Porter outlined the coming Associated Students administration for the Herald, closing the 1968-69 transition.

events.title: President Kelly Thompson announces his resignation
events.body: Thompson, who had approved the Associated Students constitution in 1966, announced he would step down as WKU's president. The Herald covered it in the same issue as the incoming Zielke-Porter student administration.

events.title: An assessment to pay for entertainment
events.body: The Herald reported that an assessment would provide funds for campus entertainment. It is the earliest reference in the archive to a dedicated student charge behind the Associated Students' concert and lecture booking; the article index does not give the amount.
events.money: amount not stated in the Herald's article index

events.title: Booking problems plague the entertainment calendar
events.body: Ellen Bennett reported that booking problems still plagued the Associated Students entertainment calendar. The same issue carried Alana White on the government's committees starting work and announced the Cinema Guild's season of art films.

events.title: An Associated Students dance, and a book exchange that was not theirs
events.body: The Herald announced an Associated Students dance for the next day. The same issue reported the Veterans book exchange a tremendous success, a reminder that the textbook service students used in these years was run by the veterans' club and not by student government.

events.title: Sam and Dave play campus on 3 December
events.body: Gail Barton reported in the Herald of 21 November that Sam and Dave would entertain on 3 December 1968. The same issue announced an Associated Students dance that Friday night and carried Bruce Tucker arguing that the lectures lacked spark and needed a student forum.

events.title: The Chattanooga Coachmen booked for an Associated Students dance
events.body: The Herald announced that an Associated Students dance would feature the Chattanooga Coachmen. The same issue reported James Farmer scheduled for the lecture series and the government's election set for the following Tuesday.

events.title: James Farmer speaks, a first for the lecture series
events.body: The Herald's election special edition of 25 March 1969 carried the notice "James Farmer Speaks Tonight." The paper had introduced the appearance the previous week under the headline "James Farmer Marks a First for Lectures." The index does not record in what way the Herald counted the founder of the Congress of Racial Equality a first for the series.

events.title: Henry Mancini in concert
events.body: Alana White announced in the Herald of 17 April that Henry Mancini would appear in concert, and the issue of 24 April set the date for that Saturday. Gail Barton and Ellen Bennett reviewed it on 1 May under the headline "Concert Sets Mood of Delight."

events.title: A committee opens a study of the campus speaker policy
events.body: Bruce Tucker reported that a committee had undertaken a study of the campus speaker policy. The question of who could be invited to Western ran through the next two years and was settled by the Board of Regents in October 1970.

events.title: Senator Mike Gravel billed for a lecture
events.body: The Herald announced Senator Mike Gravel of Alaska billed for a campus lecture in the last weeks of Bill Straeffer's term. The same issue reviewed the year under the headline "Associated Students Produces Year of Advancement."

events.title: The Association billed to open the Associated Students year
events.body: Associated Students billed a concert by the Association to open its entertainment year, announced in the Herald of 10 October 1968. The issue of 24 October carried photographs of the concert and an interview with the group, so it was played, but neither issue listing gives the night it happened.

documents.summary: Vice President Ron Beck's memo to President Kelly Thompson reporting the full results of the 2 May 1968 Associated Students and class elections, office by office with vote counts.
documents.extract: Total number of voters was 2,894 - approximately 34 percent of 8,500.

leaders.name: Paul Gerard, III
leaders.note: Second year of the two-year 1968-70 plate; see 1968-69. Resolved: the 1969 Talisman captions him "Paul Gerard, the Student Regent" and the Herald of 27 February 1969 explains the mechanism - Kentucky's 1968 law required a student regent at every state campus, and because Associated Students president Bill Straeffer was an out-of-state student, the Congress of Associated Students elected Gerard, a Bowling Green junior and junior class president, to the seat instead. He sat as a non-voting member. Contemporary sources print his name without the suffix the plaque carries.
profile: Paul Gerard entered 1969-70 as the sitting student regent, the role in which the Herald had profiled him in February 1969. The student seat still carried no vote.

The limits of the position defined the year around him: in March 1970 the Herald reported the legislature dropping the bill that would have given student regents a vote, under the headline that lawmakers had kept students impotent.

leaders.name: Larry Zielke
leaders.note: Plaque reads 1970-71, paired with John Lyne. Herald coverage places Zielke's actual term here, in 1969-70: he and Frank Genzianelli 'clash for the presidency' in the 25 March 1969 special election edition, and by 22 May 1969 the Herald reports Zielke and running mate David Porter outlining their incoming administration - the term that would open that fall. Lyne, who lost the companion 'second spot' race to Porter in the same 1969 election, went on to win the presidency unopposed in March 1970 for 1970-71 (see that year). The plaque's 1970-71 pairing of Lyne and Zielke conflates two separate one-year terms.
profile: Zielke won the Associated Students presidency in the 25 March 1969 election, beating Frank Genzianelli. David Porter won the companion vice-presidential race the same day, beating John Lyne - the two men who would face each other for the presidency the following year. By 22 May 1969 the Herald was running Zielke and Porter's own outline of their coming administration, in the same issue that covered President Kelly Thompson's resignation announcement.

The plaque records this term one year late, under 1970-71 and paired with Lyne - who did not take office until the following spring. What the Zielke-Porter administration did in office beyond the year-opening outline is not yet confirmed from the archive.

events.title: Genzianelli and Zielke clash for the presidency
events.body: The Herald's Associated Students election special edition covered a two-way presidential race between Frank Genzianelli and Larry Zielke, and a separate race for the second officer spot between John Lyne and David Porter.

events.title: Zielke and Porter outline the coming administration
events.body: With Larry Zielke elected president and David Porter as his second officer, the Herald ran their plans for the 1969-70 Associated Students administration. The same issue covered President Kelly Thompson's resignation announcement.

events.title: Associated Student Congress endorses the Vietnam Moratorium
events.body: The Herald called it a bold step. The clearest early example of the body taking a position outside the campus fence - the same argument that returns in 2017 and 2023.

events.title: Students start grading the faculty
events.body: An ASG committee compiled the results of Western's first student teacher-evaluation effort. The Herald had already editorialised demanding the tabulation move faster.

events.title: 'Associate' regents want voting power
events.body: Two pieces in one issue: Associated Students seeking voting rights for the student regent, and student and faculty 'associate' regents pressing for a vote. An editorial calls for broad support of Senate Bill 75. Two years in, the seat was still symbolic.

events.title: New constitution sent back for study
events.body: The Associated Student Government returned its proposed new constitution for further study while limiting how long the review could run. The same issue reported the group enlisting merchants for a student discount plan.

events.title: ASG urges a probe of student housing
events.body: The Associated Student Government urged an investigation of student housing, one of the fall's most pointed challenges to university policy.

events.title: Congress joins the fight against the superboard
events.body: The Associated Students Congress joined the fight against a proposed state superboard for higher education, and the Herald's editorial page argued the same week that the student regent deserved a vote.

events.title: Lyne wins the presidency before the race begins
events.body: John Lyne won the Associated Students presidency before the race began, his bid unopposed. The same issue reported the legislature dropping the bill that would have given student regents a vote, under a headline that lawmakers had kept students impotent.

events.title: Four constitution changes go to a vote
events.body: The Associated Students Congress moved to seek ratification of four constitution changes, and the Herald saluted vice president David Porter as the government's unsung hero.

events.title: ASG figures in the Kent State week delegations
events.body: During the Strike Western! demonstrations after the Kent State shootings, John Lyne and Larry Zielke were among the students who presented resolutions to President Dero Downing and Dean Charles Keown on May 8, and both sat with the group that received the university's response on May 11.

events.title: Congress endorses Downing's reply to protesters
events.body: As the Strike Western! week wound down, the Associated Student Congress unanimously endorsed President Dero Downing's reply to the protesters, aligning the elected student government with the administration's answer to the demonstrations.

events.title: Doug Alexander captures the vice presidency
events.body: Alexander beat Steve Tichenor for the Associated Students vice presidency in the vote held the week after Lyne's uncontested presidential win.

events.title: A book exchange runs at the start of term
events.body: The first Herald of 1969-70 reported that a book exchange was reducing costs for students and would close on Thursday. The same issue announced the year's lecture series and the 1969 Homecoming theme.

events.title: John Lyne questions the music preference poll
events.body: John Lyne, a year before he became president, wrote in the Herald that the Associated Students Congress's music preference poll needed closer examination. The same issue reported Congress dropping discussion of the survey's validity and an editorial warning the lecture series promised a lacklustre season.

events.title: Associated Students moves to boost the entertainment fare
events.body: The Herald reported the Associated Students moving to boost the entertainment on offer, and separately that the government's film showings were contributing an extra cultural dimension to campus. The same issue announced a new calendar to aid students and reported NBC's Chet Huntley might speak at Western.

events.title: A discount book for students
events.body: The Herald announced that the Associated Student Government would issue a discount book, and backed it with an editorial headed "Discount Offers More for Money." The same issue reported the Lettermen returning for a December concert.

events.title: Twenty-one merchants sign the discount programme
events.body: The Herald reported that twenty-one local merchants had signed with the discount programme and that the Associated Student Government and the merchants had reached a discount co-operation. The same issue carried Reginald Glass asking whether the government's entertainment was slanted.

events.title: Congress considers raising the semester head fee
events.body: The Herald reported the Associated Students considering a boost in the semester head fee, the charge that paid for its programme. The article index does not record the figure discussed.
events.money: proposed increase; amount not stated in the article index

events.title: Blood, Sweat and Tears signs an Associated Students contract
events.body: The Herald reported on 17 March 1970 that Blood, Sweat and Tears had signed a contract with the Associated Students. The group played on 25 April.

events.title: Blood, Sweat and Tears play, and the audience entertains the entertainers
events.body: The Herald of 21 April set the Blood, Sweat and Tears concert for that Saturday. The review a week later ran under the headline "Audience 'Entertains' Entertainers," the paper's verdict on how the night went.

events.title: An Associated Students dance from eight until midnight
events.body: The Herald announced an Associated Students dance running from 8 to 12 that night, alongside the Cinema '70 showing of "The Promoter."

events.title: A student discount card planned for the autumn
events.body: Don Smith reported in the Herald that a student discount card was planned for the fall term, the next step on from the discount book issued in November 1969.

events.title: Symposiums to seek the views of students
events.body: Lyda Parker reported that symposiums would seek students' views, and the following issue reported them set for the dormitories. On 20 March the Herald called the level of interest an encouraging sign, and on 27 March reported the symposiums had been very successful.

events.title: The folk festival returns on 16 April
events.body: The Herald announced that the folk festival would return on 16 April 1970. Tom Todd reported on 21 April that the Southern Folk Festival performers had met an enthusiastic reception.

leaders.name: John Lyne
leaders.note: Ran for the Associated Students' second officer spot against David Porter in the 1969 election and lost; won the presidency outright in the 1970 election, unopposed, for the 1970-71 term. The plaque's pairing with Larry Zielke under 1970-71 is wrong - Zielke's term was 1969-70; see that year.

sources.label: Herald 49:35, 13 Mar 1970 - "John Lyne Wins Presidency Before Race Begins"

profile: Lyne first ran for Associated Students office in the March 1969 election, contesting the vice-presidential ('second spot') race against David Porter and losing; Porter went on to serve as Larry Zielke's vice president for 1969-70. A year later, no one filed against Lyne for the 1970-71 presidency, and the Herald reported on 13 March 1970 that he had 'won the presidency before the race begins.' Doug Alexander won the vice presidency the same election cycle, beating Steve Tichenor, in a vote held the following week.

The term began against the backdrop of the Kent State shootings that May: the Associated Student Congress's October 1970 resolution on the women's curfew ran in a Herald issue whose letters page was dominated by students arguing about Kent State, and the same fall the Board of Regents seated eight students on the Academic Council. Beyond the curfew resolution, the Congress passed a lecture bill on 6 November 1970 funding campus appearances by William Kunstler and Bernadette Devlin, and separately endorsed a proposed new constitution two weeks later; a study committee kept refining it, reaching judicial-reform provisions by February 1971.

John Lyne was one of the most visible students on the Hill before taking office, writing a steady stream of Herald columns through 1969-70 and representing Kentuckians in the national draft lottery drawing in December 1969.
Lyne won the Associated Students presidency in March 1970 without opposition, the Herald reporting that he had captured the office before the race began.

Through 1970-71 Lyne fought his administration's corner in the Herald's letters column, complaining in January that he had been kept in the dark about an appointment and defending the Associated Students lecture series against attack that April, in the issue that reported W.S. Moss taking the oath as regent.

events.title: John Lyne wins the presidency before the race begins
events.body: No opponent filed against Lyne for the 1970-71 Associated Students presidency, and the Herald reported him elected without a contest.

events.title: Regents seat eight students on the Academic Council
events.body: An editorial framed it as the Regents opening doors to student expression in academics. Representation was arriving faster in the curriculum committees than on the board itself.

events.title: A resolution on the women's curfew, five months after Kent State
events.body: The Associated Student Congress passed a curfew resolution; the Herald reported abolition was unlikely that year and editorialised that the curfew was obsolete. The letters page in the same issue is almost entirely students arguing about Kent State.

events.title: Congress funds Kunstler and Devlin lectures, plans new constitution
events.body: The Associated Student Congress passed a lecture bill funding campus appearances by William Kunstler and Bernadette Devlin, and the Herald reported the Congress was drafting a new constitution.

events.title: Congress endorses a proposed constitution
events.body: The Associated Student Congress endorsed a proposed new constitution, continuing the reform effort launched two weeks earlier. The same issue previewed William Kunstler's scheduled Monday lecture, funded by the Congress's 6 November bill.

events.title: Constitution committee turns to judicial reform
events.body: The constitution study committee took up judicial reform provisions, the Herald reported. The same issue carried a student's published praise for William Kunstler's campus lecture.

events.title: A committee opens a constitution study
events.body: A committee was formed to study Associated Student constitutions, renewing the reform effort that had produced a second constitution the year before.

events.title: Resolutions pass; a center for students sought
events.body: Resolutions gained approval in the Associated Students Congress, and the government pressed its call for a center for students in the Herald's pages.

events.title: Twenty offices go begging
events.body: With filing open for the spring elections, the Herald reported twenty student government offices going begging for candidates.

events.title: Eighty-four to seek campus offices
events.body: By election eve the field had filled out: the Herald counted 84 students seeking campus offices in Tuesday's voting.

events.title: Linda Jones elected first woman president
events.body: Linda Jones was elected the first woman president of the Associated Student Government. The Western Alumnus pictured her being sworn in alongside faculty regent Lowell Harrison.

src.label: WKU Timeline: Linda Jones (Western Alumnus, 6 Apr 1971)

events.title: New congress leaders air the issues
events.body: The newly elected Associated Student Congress leaders aired major issues for the Herald and gave clues on what to expect in the fall.

events.title: Western hosts a conference on discount programmes
events.body: The summer Herald reported that the Associated Students would host a conference on discount programmes and that discount cards would be given out at fall registration. Western was by then teaching other Kentucky campuses how to run the scheme.

events.title: The discount card offers savings
events.body: Kaye Thomas reported in the Herald that the discount card offered savings to students. The card was handed out at registration and ran through the year; John Lyne's own account of his term said the discount programme with local merchants had been maintained.

events.title: Associated Students presents a documentary double feature
events.body: The Herald announced that the Associated Students would present documentaries in a double feature that night. It is the first clearly labelled film screening the government put on itself, separate from the subscription-based Cinema Guild.

events.title: The Ides of March draw a meagre crowd
events.body: The Herald of 29 September billed the Ides of March for that Saturday. Travis Witt's review on 6 October reported the concert had attracted a meagre crowd, one of several poor houses that made 1970-71 a difficult year for campus bookings.

events.title: The Regents put an open speaker policy into effect
events.body: Richard Morris reported that a unanimous vote from the Regents had put the new speaker policy into effect. John Lyne said afterwards that the push for an open speaker policy, from student demand through to implementation, had yielded results; it is what made the Kunstler and Devlin bookings possible.

events.title: Congress to show films for Halloween
events.body: The Herald reported the Associated Student Congress would show films for Halloween. The same issue carried a letter from Mania Ritter mourning the death of concerts on campus.

events.title: Dick Gregory speaks after a second test of the new speaker policy
events.body: David Sutherland announced in the Herald of 30 October that the civil rights comedian Dick Gregory would speak on Monday, under an editorial headed "Dick Gregory Go-Ahead Poses Second Test." Clark Hanes interviewed him on 3 November and Ernie Hearion reported his line that the fate and destiny of the nation depended on youth. The 1971 Talisman dates the appearance to 12 November; the Herald's own contemporaneous coverage places it at the start of the month.

events.title: The Temptations draw a capacity crowd
events.body: Mason Ralph announced in the Herald of 17 November that the Temptations would sing the next day. His review on 20 November reported the group drew a capacity crowd and the concert evoked mixed reactions; the 1971 Talisman said they kept a packed house hypnotised.
events.money: capacity crowd, per the Herald review

events.title: Ravi Shankar plays Western
events.body: Mason Ralph announced on 4 December that Ravi Shankar was coming that Wednesday, and the 8 December issue put the sitar player in the concert spotlight for the following night. Lyne cited Shankar as proof that the government was bringing names that were not of the top forty variety.

events.title: Julian Bond speaks on a Sunday
events.body: Clark Hanes reported in the Herald of 11 December that the Georgia legislator Julian Bond would speak that Sunday. The 1971 Talisman lists Bond on 13 December among the more controversial speakers the Associated Students brought to campus.

events.title: William Kunstler speaks after a delay
events.body: The Herald of 20 November 1970 had billed the Chicago Seven lawyer to speak that Monday; he did not appear until the new year. The paper announced on 29 January that Kunstler was set to speak, and Peggy Kirkpatrick's piece on 2 February headed "Courtroom Paladin to Speak Thursday" carried the date. The 1971 Talisman shows Lyne hosting him on campus.

events.title: Bernadette Devlin speaks on a Friday night
events.body: The Herald announced the Irish MP's lecture on 19 February, called her an Irish firebrand on 23 February, and ran "Irish Socialist Speaks Tonight" on the day itself. Her appearance and Kunstler's were funded by a lecture bill the Associated Student Congress passed the previous November.

events.title: Neil Diamond in concert
events.body: The Herald of 26 February announced that the pop vocalist Neil Diamond would present a concert that Thursday. The 1971 Talisman lists Diamond and the Trinidad-Tripoli Steel Band as the spring entertainment.

events.title: S. I. Hayakawa lectures
events.body: The Herald announced on 30 March that Dr S. I. Hayakawa would lecture that Thursday. The 1971 Talisman lists him with Kunstler and Devlin as the spring speakers the Associated Students had scheduled.

events.title: A weekly radio programme on the government's work
events.body: The 1971 Talisman reported that, to promote better communication between students and their government, Lyne set up a weekly radio programme to tell of the Associated Students' work. The Herald front page reproduced in the yearbook records him saying the programme could be started within the hour.

events.title: Pacific Gas and Electric panned after Homecoming weekend
events.body: Pacific Gas and Electric played at Western as part of Homecoming weekend in October 1970. Ernie Hearion reviewed the show in the Herald of 13 October under the heading "Utilities Down Sharply on Entertainment Market", and the 1971 Talisman said the group won over very few of the crowd. The same yearbook recorded that the Herald was outspoken that year about the entertainment on which the Associated Students chose to spend students' activity funds.

src.label: College Heights Herald 50:13, 13 Oct 1970 (review); 1971 Talisman, Homecoming and Concerts

events.title: Associated Students co-sponsored the musical '1776'
events.body: The Herald of 6 October 1970 announced that the curtain would rise the next day on the Broadway musical '1776'. Writing in the 1971 Talisman, Associated Students president John Lyne listed the co-sponsorship of '1776' among the theatrical events his government had backed as it widened its work from entertainment into cultural programmes. The same yearbook places the performance among that week's Homecoming activities.

events.title: Lyne's account: entertainment becomes a cultural programme
events.body: In a signed statement in the 1971 Talisman, president John Lyne wrote that the entertainment side of Associated Students had been expanded into a cultural programmes concept, that big-name concerts continued but names outside the top forty such as Ravi Shankar had been brought in, and that theatrical events had been sponsored, including the co-sponsorship of "1776". He recorded a student-run lecture series as that year's significant addition, said the student discount programme with local merchants had been maintained, and said the organisation was working towards a legal service for students that would include a legal defence fund and a student advocates' corps.

src.label: 1971 Talisman, pp. 66-67, signed statement by John Lyne

executive.name: John Lyne
executive.note: Unopposed.

executive.name: Doug Alexander
executive.note: Beat Steve Tichenor.

leaders.name: Linda Jones
leaders.note: First woman to hold the office. The WKU Timeline dates her election to 6 April 1971, matching the plaque year. The Herald of 28 April 1972 carries a piece headed 'Jones, Linda. Reflects on Term' in the same issue as a strike call over dorm visitation.
profile: Jones was elected the first woman president of the Associated Student Government on 6 April 1971; the Western Alumnus photographed her being sworn in with faculty regent Lowell Harrison by Georgia Bates.

That fall, on 14 September 1971, the Herald reported the Associated Students affiliating with a wider student association, though the article index alone does not identify which body. By 1 February 1972, four years after the student regent seat was created, the Herald was still reporting the seat had no vote.

Through February and March 1972, Jones's Congress pushed a rewritten constitution: it voted section by section on 22 February, when the Herald printed the executive branch's full text, and the Herald reported the executive branch accepted on 29 February. The same 29 February issue reported the Kentucky Civil Liberties Union planning court action connected to Associated Students and The Fly, a separate WKU underground newspaper, and carried Jones's own piece, 'Associated Students Corrects Herald', a public correction of the paper's coverage of the organization. The archive does not yet hold the text of either the KCLU piece or Jones's correction, so the underlying dispute and what she corrected both remain unconfirmed.

Days earlier, the Herald's 25 February 1972 issue ran under the headline 'Chaos Reigns at Associated Students Meeting', alongside a separate piece arguing that student interest in the organization had collapsed and the Associated Students had followed it down.

The constitution went to referendum at the end of March: the Herald's 28 March issue urged students to 'Vote Yes' ahead of a two-day vote, and Associated Students formally endorsed the Kentucky Civil Liberties Union's lawsuit in the same issue. The archive does not yet show the referendum's result or turnout.

Her term closed on 28 April 1972 as a Mass Action Committee called for a strike over dorm visitation and the Associated Students installed its next officers; the same issue reported students had won six votes on a university council, and carried Jones's own reflection on her year in office.

events.title: Linda Jones elected first woman ASG president
events.body: Jones became the first woman elected president of the Associated Student Government. A photograph in the Western Alumnus shows her being sworn in alongside faculty regent Lowell Harrison by Georgia Bates.

events.title: Associated Students affiliates with a wider student association
events.body: An early attempt to gain leverage beyond the Hill. Which body it joined is not clear from the article index alone.

events.title: 'Student Regent May Get Vote'
events.body: Four years after the seat was created it was still non-voting. The same issue has the Academic Council clarifying grievance procedure and an Associated Students open session scheduled for 12 February.

events.title: 'Chaos Reigns at Associated Students Meeting'
events.body: The same issue carries students planning a petition to force dorm visitation and a separate piece arguing student interest had collapsed and the Associated Students had followed it down.

events.title: Congress votes on a section of the new constitution; full text published
events.body: The Associated Students Congress voted on a section of the proposed constitution, and the Herald printed the full text of the document's proposed executive branch alongside the vote coverage.

events.title: Executive branch of a revised constitution accepted
events.body: The Herald reported acceptance of the executive branch of a revised Associated Students constitution. The archive does not yet hold the article's text or what changed.

events.title: Kentucky Civil Liberties Union plans court action on behalf of Associated Students
events.body: The Herald reported the Kentucky Civil Liberties Union planning court action on behalf of Associated Students, under a headline that also named The Fly, a separate WKU underground newspaper active that year. The archive does not yet hold the article's text, so the underlying dispute is not yet confirmed.

events.title: Linda Jones publicly corrects the Herald
events.body: President Linda Jones wrote a piece headlined 'Associated Students Corrects Herald', a public correction of the paper's own reporting on the organization. The archive does not yet hold the article's text or what it corrected.

events.title: 'Vote Yes' campaign for the new constitution; referendum set
events.body: The Herald carried a piece by Nancy Pape urging students to 'Vote Yes' on the Associated Students constitution ahead of a referendum set for the next two days, in the same issue that advertised an Associated Students mini-concert.

events.title: Associated Students endorses the Kentucky Civil Liberties Union lawsuit
events.body: The Herald reported that Associated Students formally endorsed the Kentucky Civil Liberties Union's lawsuit, a month after the Herald first reported the union planning court action connected to the organization and The Fly.

events.title: A strike threat over visitation, and six votes won on a university council
events.body: A Mass Action Committee called for a strike over dorm visitation while the Associated Students installed next year's officers. Buried in the same issue: students gained six votes on a university council. Linda Jones reflected on her term.

events.title: The Trinidad Steel Band and the Serendipity Singers
events.body: The Herald previewed the double bill on 14 September as "Folk Rock vs Steel Band in Thursday Concert" and Kim Weaver's review on 21 September was headed "Steel Band Betters Singers in Concert." The 1972 Talisman calls it the first major Associated Students sponsored concert of the year and says student requests had brought the steel band back for a second consecutive year.

events.title: Benjamin Spock, the first Associated Students speaker of the year
events.body: The Herald of 21 September announced Dr Benjamin Spock lecturing on campus that Thursday. The 1972 Talisman records that Spock, the first speaker sponsored by the Associated Students that year, attacked the United States role in Vietnam and drew a crowd of about 1,100.

events.title: Ike and Tina Turner headline Homecoming before about 12,000
events.body: The 1972 Talisman reports the Ike and Tina Turner Revue performing before an estimated crowd of 12,000 in Diddle Arena at the Homecoming concert, backed by the eight-member Kings of Rhythm. The Herald of 19 October ran "Concert Lovers Buoyed by Turnout for Ike & Tina Turner" alongside a letter from Phyllis Sower repulsed at the actions of a student at the Friday night concert. It was the high point of the Associated Students' concert year.
events.money: estimated crowd of 12,000 in Diddle Arena

events.title: A mock election for governor draws 1,175 votes
events.body: The Associated Students ran a mock gubernatorial election on 21 October 1971. The 1972 Talisman records that only 1,175 of Western's 11,000 students voted and that they elected the Republican Tom Emberton; the Herald reported the result on 22 October. Kentucky's voters chose Wendell Ford by a substantial margin on 2 November.

events.title: First Gear plays a mini-concert
events.body: The Herald of 22 October reported First Gear featured for a mini-concert. The 1972 Talisman shows Larnelle Harris of First Gear on stage at an Associated Students sponsored mini-concert; the Persuasions and Supa were among the other groups that autumn.

events.title: Supa brings a jamboree to Western
events.body: The Herald announced on 29 October that the Associated Students had set a mini-concert with Supa for the next day, and Roger Miller's review on 2 November was headed "Mini-Concert Doesn't Mean Mini-Talent." A letter from Brent Ferguson the same week praised the Associated Students mini-concerts.

events.title: The government goes after rock groups
events.body: Travis Witt reported in the Herald that the Associated Students were contacting rock groups. The 1972 Talisman names Leon Russell, Mountain, Alice Cooper and It's a Beautiful Day as the acts approached after students asked for bigger names.

events.title: Mountain and Black Oak Arkansas cancelled the day before the show
events.body: The Herald billed two rock groups for a 2 December Associated Students concert on 12 November and named Mountain and Black Oak Arkansas on 19 November. The 1972 Talisman records that on 2 December, the day before the engagement, student government leaders were forced to cancel because Mountain's lead singer Felix Pappalardi was ill. A letter from Terry Gatlin questioning the cancellation ran in the Herald of 10 December.

events.title: A surprise mini-concert with Friction
events.body: Roger Miller reported in the Herald that a surprise mini-concert on the Wednesday had hot music by Friction. It came the week after the Mountain and Black Oak Arkansas cancellation.

events.title: The Legal Rights Committee runs a symposium with lawyers
events.body: Stephanie Madison reported that the Associated Students Legal Rights Committee was planning a symposium with lawyers for 1 December. Carter Pence's report on 3 December, "Students Air Complaints at Symposium," covered the event.

events.title: The Cellar, the Associated Students teahouse, opens
events.body: Roger Miller announced the opening in the Herald under the headline "Another First: the Cellar, Associated Students Teahouse, Opens Friday." The paper covered it again a week later as "Cellar-Dwellers" and reported the campus teahouse stirred mixed emotions; by the end of April the Herald was calling it a dimly lit teahouse that outshone the government's other efforts. The 1972 Talisman describes it as a coffee house in West Hall.

events.title: A free calendar for students
events.body: The Herald reported that the Associated Students were offering a free calendar, and Joe Huggins announced it again on 21 January. The same issue reported the government scheduling lectures, concerts and a film series for the second semester.

events.title: Art Buchwald lectures
events.body: Roger Miller reported that the humour columnist Art Buchwald would lecture that night. The 1972 Talisman records his lecture as "Art Buchwald at Large" and says it combined personal anecdotes with political commentary; he stayed afterwards to talk with students.

events.title: James J. Kilpatrick speaks
events.body: Reginald Glass announced in the Herald that the syndicated columnist James J. Kilpatrick would speak that night. The 1972 Talisman records him describing the youth vote as a real problem for the Republicans.

events.title: The Associated Students movie series opens with King Kong
events.body: The Herald announced that the Associated Students movie series would open the next day with "King Kong," and an editorial three days later said the series could be a hit. The 1972 Talisman lists the Gaslight film series among the government's new entertainment; the Herald of 2 May had W. C. Fields in "The Flying Ace" set for Gaslight.

events.title: The Jake Jones mini-concert is cancelled
events.body: The Herald reported that the Associated Students had cancelled the Jake Jones mini-concert set for 29 January. The same issue carried a letter from Anthony Kinzel disconcerted with the government.

events.title: A cancelled Lennon and Ono screening brings a furious postbag
events.body: The Herald of 28 January had announced John Lennon and Yoko Ono films for the following week. On 4 February the paper printed three letters about the cancellation, one from a student who wanted to see the Lennon film and two headed "Disappointed at Film Cancellation" and "Furious at Film Cancellation," alongside Roger Miller reporting the Associated Students Congress reacting to censorship.

events.title: Norman Mailer lectures
events.body: Roger Miller announced in the Herald of 8 February that Norman Mailer's lecture was slated for the following night. The 1972 Talisman records the author and social critic telling his audience that amateurism was replacing professionalism.

events.title: Four sent to the entertainment conference
events.body: Jill Flanders reported that Reginald Glass, Mike Fiorella, Ron Beck and Jim Schmidt attended an entertainment conference. The 1972 Talisman explains the machinery behind the year's programme: Ron Beck was unit co-ordinator for the state branch of the National Entertainment Conference, ten schools were represented, the state body met on the Western campus in both semesters for programming workshops, and the three mini-concerts each semester were the result.

events.title: The Isaac Hayes concert is cancelled
events.body: Carter Pence reported the cancellation in the Herald of 18 February. The 1972 Talisman says the 17 February concert failed to materialise because Hayes was suffering from flu, and that he later contacted Western to reschedule.

events.title: Benjamin Mays on two decades of human rights
events.body: The Herald announced the black educator's lecture on 25 February and ran "Benjamin Mays Speaks Tonight" on 29 February. The 1972 Talisman gives his subject as "Two Decades of Human Rights"; the yearbook's caption says he spoke on 29 February while its running text says only that he was scheduled to.

events.title: Edwin Reischauer, former ambassador to Japan
events.body: The Herald announced that the former ambassador would speak that night. The same issue reported that the Associated Students would present "The Fantasticks" and carried an editorial headed "Herald Salutes Associated Students."

events.title: The Imperials play a mini-concert
events.body: The Herald of 11 April announced that the Thursday Associated Students mini-concert would feature the Imperials.

events.title: The Carpenters in Diddle Arena
events.body: The Herald of 14 April announced that the Carpenters would appear in concert the following Tuesday. The 1972 Talisman confirms the brother and sister recording act appeared in Diddle Arena on 18 April; they had been promised to students back in October alongside Mountain, Black Oak Arkansas and Isaac Hayes.

events.title: It's a Beautiful Day and If close the concert year
events.body: The Herald of 20 April announced a rock concert for the following Thursday with It's a Beautiful Day and If. Reginald Glass wrote the preview "Beautiful Day, If Headline Concert" in the issue of 25 April.

events.title: The Cellar finishes the year the best thing the government did
events.body: The Herald of 28 April reported the Cellar's finals were set and ran a piece headed "Cellar: It's Only a Dimly Lit Teahouse but Outshines Other Associated Student Government Efforts." The same issue reported a concert highlighting the Folk Arts Festival and the installation of next year's officers.

events.title: Finances and scheduling name the problem
events.body: The Herald ran a piece headed "Finances, Scheduling Pose Problems in Entertainment" in the week of Homecoming. Over the following month the paper printed an editorial arguing the benefits outweighed the risks in scheduling big concerts and letters from students wanting bigger concerts and disputing the paper's handling of the entertainment question.

events.title: Reginald Glass signs the Associated Students' entertainment contracts
events.body: The 1972 Talisman photographed Reginald Glass, vice-president of Associated Students, signing a speaker contract, and said signing contracts for concerts and speakers was one of his responsibilities. The first speaker the Associated Students sponsored was Dr Benjamin Spock. Its other activities that year included bringing in the Trinidad Steel Band, Ike and Tina Turner and several mini-concerts, sponsoring the Homecoming dance, and running a mock election before the Kentucky governor's race.

events.title: The Emme Kemp Jazz Trio opens the ASG mini-concert season
events.body: The Herald reported on 31 August 1971 that the Kemp Trio had set a concert. The 1972 Talisman recorded that the Associated Students entertained students with several mini-concerts that fall semester, small-scale shows meant to give top quality entertainment at less cost and presented in cooperation with other Kentucky colleges, and that the season started with the Emme Kemp Jazz Trio; student requests then brought the Trinidad Steel Band back with the Serendipity Singers.

events.title: Associated Students rescheduled the Isaac Hayes concert
events.body: The Isaac Hayes concert set for 17 February 1972 fell through when Hayes had flu, and the 1972 Talisman records that Associated Students rescheduled it for 23 March. Stephanie Madison's review in the Herald of 28 March shows the rescheduled show went ahead.

events.title: The year's programme summed up in the yearbook
events.body: The 1972 Talisman summarised Linda Jones's year under the heading "A.S. makes great strides in implementing new programs": in entertainment, mini-concerts, a coffee house in West Hall and the Gaslight film series joined several top-name musical groups and lecturers. The same volume records that Associated Students conducted the elections for class officers, Who's Who and Homecoming queen, held the October mock election for governor, ran a symposium at which students could question administrators, sponsored the Homecoming dance, and revived the Kentucky Student Association among the state's student governments, with several meetings held at Western.
events.money: 1,175 of Western's 11,000 students voted in the 21 October mock election

src.label: 1972 Talisman, Associated Students sections, pp. 57 and 272-73

leaders.name: Edward Jordan, Jr.
leaders.note: Confirmed by direct Herald election coverage: he ran on a platform the paper labeled progressivism, beat Bob Hatfield in the 20 April 1972 election, and the Herald reported the win five days later. Paired on the plaque with Michael Fiorella, the student regent that year.
profile: Jordan ran for the Associated Student Government presidency on a platform the Herald's Roger Miller labeled progressivism, profiled a week before the vote. Congress had separately voted to place his opponent, Bob Hatfield, on the ballot after a dispute over Hatfield's eligibility.

Jordan beat Hatfield in the 20 April 1972 election; the Herald reported his win on 25 April under the headline 'Ed Jordan Wins Top Office,' in the same issue as an editorial by Pence and Carter arguing the new ASG president needed cooperation and support.

Edward Jordan's name entered the Herald's letters columns on November 7, 1972, when he and Charles Boteler urged readers to restore ideals. The digitized index does not label the ASG office Jordan held.
On April 10, 1973, as top ASG offices went on the line in the spring election, a letter praising Ed Jordan ran in the Herald.
Jordan stayed in student politics after his year: in April 1974 he wrote to the Herald judging Steve Henry the most qualified candidate in that spring's races.

leaders.name: Michael Fiorella
leaders.note: Student regent, not president. Sworn in 26 September 1972 alongside gubernatorial appointees Gerald Edds and Chalmer Embry, who Gov. Wendell Ford had named the previous month.
profile: In September 1972 the Herald profiled Michael Fiorella, the Associated Student Government vice president, under the headline that he was anti-apathy.
A week later the Herald reported that Fiorella had won the student seat on the Board of Regents.
Fiorella was sworn in on September 26, 1972, alongside Gerald Edds and Chalmer Embry, the board's two other new members.

events.title: Gov. Wendell Ford names two regents
events.body: Gerald Edds and Chalmer Embry. The same issue reports the best ASG course evaluation yet, students questioning the $5 car registration fee, and filing opening for ASG offices.

events.title: Three new regents sworn in, one of them a student
events.body: Michael Fiorella took the student seat alongside Edds and Embry. The same issue reports 'Slack Time at Associated Student Government Congress', an ASG bankruptcy plan and the open-dorm visitation fight continuing.

events.title: A year of involvement promised
events.body: The Herald opened the year reporting Associated Student Government plans for a year of involvement, in an issue that also covered the regents approving a five dollar vehicle registration fee.

events.title: Course evaluation called the best yet
events.body: The Herald judged ASG's course evaluation the best yet, as filing opened for fall ASG offices.

events.title: Five file for student regent; cheerleader ruling deplored
events.body: Five students filed for the student seat on the Board of Regents. In the same issue, an ASG resolution deplored a cheerleader ruling as the university bowed to Black students' demands after a bitter squabble over squad selection.

events.title: Funds fly as Chicago is booked
events.body: ASG funds flew as the group set a Chicago concert, corrected a tactical error by adding more polls to a campus vote, and made its student activity card available.

events.title: Fiorella wins the regent seat
events.body: Michael Fiorella, the Associated Student Government vice president, won the student seat on the Board of Regents. Days earlier the Herald had profiled him as anti-apathy.

events.title: ASG rejects Downing's position on Black affairs
events.body: The Associated Student Government rejected President Dero Downing's position on an Office of Black Affairs, one of the sharpest confrontations of the fall. A congressman's letter the same day called criticism of ASG unjustified.

events.title: Students as campus cops
events.body: ASG wanted students serving as campus police, the Herald reported, while the editorial page argued more time was needed between elections.

events.title: Top offices on the line
events.body: Top Associated Student Government offices went on the line in the day's election, and a letter writer praised Ed Jordan as the voting opened.

events.title: Ed Jordan's theme is progressivism
events.body: The Herald profiled presidential candidate Ed Jordan ahead of the ASG election, describing his campaign theme as progressivism.

events.title: Jordan and Hatfield face off for the presidency
events.body: Ed Jordan and Bob Hatfield contested the ASG presidency in the day's election, after Congress had voted to place Hatfield on the ballot. The same issue carried both candidates' comments on key election issues.

events.title: Jordan wins the presidency
events.body: The Herald reported Ed Jordan's win under the headline 'Ed Jordan Wins Top Office,' alongside an editorial by Pence and Carter arguing the new ASG president needed cooperation and support to succeed.

events.title: ASG sponsors a book exchange, fights a recycling ordinance
events.body: Associated Student Government sponsored a student book exchange. The same issue reported a city recycling ordinance had left ASG holding the bag on trash collection for its paper-recycling program.

events.title: ASG considers aid to a North Vietnam hospital
events.body: Associated Student Government considered sending aid to a hospital in North Vietnam, the Herald's Carter Pence reported, as the Paris Peace Accords negotiations neared their end.

events.title: Registration week grows into a street dance and two mini-concerts
events.body: ASG expanded its registration week programme in autumn 1972 to include a street dance and two mini-concerts. The Talisman counted this among the activities of the Activities Committee under vice president Mike Fiorella.

events.title: ASG activity card goes on sale
events.body: The Herald announced that the ASG activity card was available. The Talisman described it as a programme begun two years earlier that admitted part-time students and the spouses of students to ASG activities for a nominal charge.

events.title: Chicago plays a free concert
events.body: ASG presented Chicago on 4 October 1972 as a free concert, with pianist Robert Lamm fronting the horn section. The Talisman called it one of the season's hottest entertainment nights and said the band was soon forgotten once Jethro Tull arrived three weeks later.

events.title: Buffalo Bob Smith revives the Howdy Doody show in Van Meter
events.body: ASG brought Buffalo Bob Smith and his revival of the Howdy Doody show to Van Meter Auditorium in October 1972. The Talisman called the two-and-a-half hour programme professional and a huge success, with Smith leading a rendition of 'Clarabell the Clown' and playing Chopin, Mozart and Bach.

events.title: Jethro Tull sells tickets and loses money
events.body: Ian Anderson brought Jethro Tull to Diddle Arena on 26 October 1972. Many in the audience called it the best concert ever staged at Western, but the Talisman recorded that the pay concert was a major financial loss for ASG.
events.money: a major financial loss for ASG, amount not stated

events.title: Pat Paulsen opens the lecture programme at Homecoming
events.body: ASG sponsored the political comedian Pat Paulsen on the evening of 1 November 1972, in Homecoming week, with a lecture titled 'Pat Paulsen Looks at the 70's'. The Talisman recorded that ASG's lecture programme for the year began with him.

events.title: The Beach Boys disappoint on Homecoming Friday
events.body: ASG sponsored the Beach Boys in Diddle Arena on Friday 3 November 1972. Students had come to hear the music of the sixties and heard little of it; the Talisman reported the concert was not well received until the band turned to its golden oldies, and that many went home disappointed.

events.title: ASG Homecoming Dance closes the day
events.body: The ASG Homecoming Dance in the Garrett Conference Center Ballroom concluded the full day of Homecoming activities on 4 November 1972. It followed the game against Middle Tennessee and the reception in Diddle Arena.

events.title: Orphan plays a mini-concert to a poor crowd
events.body: The rock band Orphan played an ASG mini-concert on the Wednesday night of 15 November 1972. Al Cross reviewed it for the Herald under the headline that Orphan gave a bad crowd good music.

events.title: ASG loses money on the fall concerts
events.body: Al Cross reported in the Herald that ASG had lost money on its fall concerts. The Talisman confirmed the loss on fall entertainment without giving a figure, and the shortfall shaped the argument over the head fee that ran into the spring.
events.money: loss on fall concerts, figure not given in the sources consulted

events.title: Four free mini-concerts and the Cellar coffee house
events.body: ASG provided four free mini-concerts over the year, by Voice of Cheese, Tiny Alice, Orphan, and Rolfe Kempf with David McHugh. Weekend performances at the Cellar coffee house in West Hall rounded out the music ASG offered; the Talisman counted seven mini-concerts across the year in all.

events.title: The ASG Newsletter finally appears
events.body: After two years in the planning stages, the ASG Newsletter began publication with the November 1972 issue. It came out monthly and was meant to keep students aware of what was happening on campus.

events.title: ASG takes up the idea of a Free University
events.body: The Herald reported that ASG would consider establishing a Free University. The programme of no-cost, no-credit evening courses in subjects such as knitting, photography and yoga began the following spring under coordinator Glenn Jackson.

events.title: ASG schedules a venereal disease symposium
events.body: ASG scheduled a symposium on venereal disease, run in cooperation with Operation Venus and billed as 'V.D. Day'. The Talisman recorded that it was open to Western students, high school students and the public.

events.title: ASG announces a book exchange
events.body: The Herald reported that ASG would begin a book exchange. Congress had passed a bill to initiate a textbook exchange on campus, and the exchange ran at the start of the spring semester.

events.title: Student discount programme runs a sixth year
events.body: ASG's student discount programme continued for a sixth year, contracting with Bowling Green merchants who gave discounts to students. Plans were made to return to a discount coupon book alongside the discount card to increase use of the service.

events.title: Dance opens the spring season to two-thirds of a ballroom
events.body: ASG opened the spring semester on 2 February 1973 with the rock group Dance in the Garrett Ballroom. The Talisman said the mixture of blues-soul, Latin rock and hard rock made it hard to stay seated, but no more than two-thirds of the seats were filled.

events.title: Few attend the ASG symposiums
events.body: The Herald reported that few students attended the ASG symposiums. The venereal disease symposium had been the flagship of the series.

events.title: Stevie Wonder draws 3,850 and costs ASG up to $5,000
