events.body: ASG presented Stevie Wonder with Billy Paul and Whole Oats as the first major concert of the second semester, on Tuesday 13 February 1973. The reviews said Wonder was wondrous, but only 3,850 were on hand and ASG lost between $4,000 and $5,000.

events.title: Buckminster Fuller lectures on 'Humans in the Universe'
events.body: The University Lecture Series and ASG jointly sponsored Buckminster Fuller, who spoke on 'Humans in the Universe' on 27 February 1973. The same joint series brought Steve Atlas of Nader's Raiders, who addressed about forty-five ASG Congress members and other interested people.

events.title: Coretta Scott King and Betty Friedan speak on the joint lecture series
events.body: Coretta Scott King and Betty Friedan were both sponsored by the 1972-73 University Lecture Series and ASG. King lectured on excerpts from her book on men's freedoms and their responsibilities; Friedan, called the mother superior of women's lib, spoke on women's liberation. The Talisman does not date either lecture.

events.title: Free University adds seven classes
events.body: The Herald reported that the Free University planned to add seven new classes. The programme of free evening courses was in its first semester.

events.title: Ron Beck calls a concert a mistake
events.body: Al Cross reported in the Herald that Ron Beck, the assistant dean of student affairs who handled concert booking, called a concert a mistake. Beck's judgment on which acts belonged on campus was the standing constraint on ASG's programme for the rest of the decade.

events.title: Congress votes a referendum on raising the head fee
events.body: ASG Congress voted to hold a student referendum on raising the head fee, a week after a Herald editorial argued the fee needed a boost to insure the quality of ASG entertainment. The regents instead voted an increase in ASG's allotment that August.

events.title: Lester Flatt headlines the Bluegrass Festival
events.body: ASG closed its season on 29 April 1973 with a Bluegrass and Folk Crafts Festival headlined by Lester Flatt and the Nashville Grass, with Mac Wiseman and II Generation. It was the second consecutive year the festival had been held.

events.title: ASG announces a paper recycling project
events.body: The Herald of 6 October 1972 reported that Associated Student Government would launch a paper recycling project. The 1973 Talisman recorded that the project ran: paper was collected in ecology trash cans set at points across campus, collection was later extended to cans and bottles, and the money from the sale of recycled paper went back into the work of the Environmental Committee, which Joe Cheak headed.

events.title: Jimmy Buffett played an ASG mini-concert
events.body: The Herald of 17 April 1973 billed a mini-concert by Jimmy Buffett for that Thursday. The 1973 Talisman records that Buffett came to campus on 19 April in levis and a cowboy shirt carrying two Martin guitars, and counts him among the two major concerts, three mini-concerts and Bluegrass Festival that ASG sponsored that spring semester.

leaders.name: Steven Yater
leaders.note: Confirmed by the Herald's own 16 April 1974 retrospective, 'Presidency Ends for Steve Yater; One Major Program Started,' which places his presidency closing out at the end of the 1973-74 year, matching the plaque term.
profile: Steve Yater led the Associated Student Government through 1973-74. Early in his term he publicly commended the Board of Regents in the Herald, weeks after the board had increased ASG's budget allotment.

Yater's win was reported in the Herald's 13 April 1973 election returns; the same issue profiled him as making a good impression in his first contact with Congress and stressing a calm approach to the office. Carter Pence's companion article covered new officers being installed at a Congress party the same week, though the archive index does not yet name who besides Yater took office.
In April 1974, stung by election-season criticism, President Yater defended his administration in a letter to the Herald.
His final weeks in office stayed argumentative: the Herald of April 30 carried dueling letters under the heading 'Linda Jones vs. Steven Yater' as the student regent race closed out the year.

The Herald's own retrospective on his term, by Al Cross, ran 16 April 1974 under the headline 'Presidency Ends for Steve Yater; One Major Program Started' - the archive does not yet hold the article's text, only its headline crediting his administration with a single major accomplishment.

events.title: Yater wins the presidency; new officers installed
events.body: The Herald reported Steve Yater's win in the spring election under 'Associated Student Government Election Returns,' profiling him as making a good impression in his first Congress contact and stressing a calm approach. The same issue covered new officers being installed at a Congress party.

events.title: Gregory McKinney sworn in as WKU's first African American student regent
events.body: Seven years before Julius Price became the first Black gubernatorial appointee to the board in 1981. The student seat integrated the Board of Regents first.

events.title: Regents raise the ASG allotment
events.body: The Herald opened the year reporting a budget bulge: the Board of Regents voted to increase the Associated Student Government allotment. A companion piece introduced freshmen to ASG under the headline 'Every College Has One.'

events.title: Free University continues, smaller
events.body: ASG's Free University of no-cost, no-credit evening courses continued for another year, though with fewer courses than before.

events.title: Housing survey urges dorm improvements
events.body: An ASG housing survey urged improvement in dormitory conditions, part of a fall agenda that also included a committee on part-time student opportunities and a push for paper recycling.

events.title: A congressman resigns in protest
events.body: ASG representative Reginald Glass resigned his post in protest, the Herald reported, an early sign of strain inside the congress.

events.title: Sam Ervin booked for April
events.body: ASG contracted Senator Sam Ervin, chairman of the Senate Watergate committee, to speak at Western on April 2. The same issue reported ASG acting to revamp its committees.

events.title: Spending limit stays
events.body: ASG voted to retain its campaign spending limit rather than loosen the cap on campaign outlays.

events.title: Consolo and Henry win the election
events.body: Jeff Consolo and Steve Henry won the spring ASG election, in a cycle whose primary the Herald said showed Greek influence. Henry resigned his post over the student discount program after the results.

events.title: Five file for the student regent seat
events.body: Five students filed for the student seat on the Board of Regents ahead of the spring vote, the position that carried a place at the board table.

events.title: Herald retrospective closes out Yater's presidency
events.body: Al Cross wrote the Herald's retrospective on Steve Yater's term, headlined 'Presidency Ends for Steve Yater; One Major Program Started.' The same issue reported the regent post election set for the following week.

events.title: An $11,000 budget increase pays for the concert and lecture year
events.body: The Board of Regents approved an $11,000 increase in the student affairs budget allocated to ASG in place of a proposed head fee rise. President Steve Yater said the increase was better than a higher head fee because it took no additional money from students' pockets, and the Talisman credited it with paying for the Doobie Brothers, Seals and Crofts and the mini-concerts.

events.title: Street dance and Ginger open the year at the amphitheatre
events.body: ASG began the year with the traditional street dance during registration week, then followed a few days later with the rock band Ginger in a mini-concert at the outdoor amphitheatre. It was the first outdoor performance at the fine arts amphitheatre and the first of the year's mini-concert series.

events.title: Stringbean headlines the second Bluegrass Festival
events.body: The second Bluegrass Festival was held on 6 September 1973 with the Hee Haw star Stringbean and other Nashville acts. The Herald reported five days later that a country-western 'git-together' had replaced the bluegrass festival.

events.title: Ethos plays the second mini-concert
events.body: The electronic-rock group Ethos from Fort Wayne, Indiana, played ASG's second mini-concert on 13 October 1973 in Van Meter Auditorium. Guitarist Bill Sharpe told the boogie-oriented audience that most of the boogies would have to be in their noses; the band was warmly received and returned in the spring as an off-campus support act.

events.title: Homecoming rock and roll revival: Jerry Lee Lewis cancels and Chuck Berry never shows
events.body: ASG's first attempt at a major concert, a 1950s Rock and Roll Revival for Homecoming, collapsed twice. Jerry Lee Lewis was first booked and cancelled over management problems, Chuck Berry was signed in his place and then took an unscheduled holiday in Las Vegas and ignored the date, leaving Gary U.S. Bonds to headline with the Crystals, Freddie Cannon and Lloyd Price. Ron Beck warned the crowd before the show and offered refunds to anyone who left within fifteen minutes, and he and ASG were still trying to recover the refund money from producer Richard Nader months later.

events.title: Red Snapper plays the ASG Homecoming dance
events.body: The Homecoming dance sponsored by ASG ran from 8pm to midnight after the game against Morehead, with music by Red Snapper. Homecoming 1973 took its theme from the movies and drew a crowd of 19,500 to the game in the rain.

events.title: A student takes the concert complaints to Congress
events.body: Tony Agee, a junior from Albany, brought his and his friends' grievances before the ASG Congress at the meeting of 29 October 1973. He charged that ASG had misrepresented facts, used false advertising and put incompetent people in charge of booking; president Steve Yater blamed the producer of the Homecoming revival.

events.title: Amnesty is the least successful mini-concert of the series
events.body: The soul-blues-jazz combo Amnesty played a mini-concert in Van Meter. The Talisman said much of the crowd enjoyed it but that it was the least successful show of the mini-concert series.

events.title: The Doobie Brothers play to 6,000
events.body: The Doobie Brothers played Diddle Arena on 4 December 1973 before a crowd of 6,000. The group had originally been booked for October and was postponed over a recording commitment; the Herald called the show average but the Talisman said it pleased most of the crowd.

events.title: Seals and Crofts play the first free concert in more than a year
events.body: Seals and Crofts opened the spring semester on Saturday 19 January 1974 before what the 1974 Talisman called one of the largest crowds ever to see a show in Diddle Arena. The Talisman called it in some ways the best campus concert in more than a year and the first free concert since the autumn of 1972, scheduling and money having prevented one since.

events.title: The Free University shuts down after two semesters
events.body: The Herald reported that the Free U had shut down after two semesters. Coordinator Glenn Jackson blamed a lack of student interest and the difficulty of finding people to teach the classes, which had covered knitting, photography, yoga and other subjects.

events.title: ASG considers ending the legal loan fund
events.body: The Herald reported that ASG might end its legal loan fund. The Legal Rights Committee had been working towards a bail-bond fund for arrested students and had taken up drug expulsions, the refusal to show X-rated films in the student center and the 'Fly' censorship case.

events.title: Raymond McNally lectures on Dracula
events.body: ASG brought Dr Raymond McNally of Boston College, co-author of 'In Search of Dracula', to lecture on vampirism before a large audience in the Garrett Conference Center Ballroom. He traced the legend to a fifteenth century Romanian prince and showed clips from vampire films.

events.title: Harry Chapin opens the major-mini concert series
events.body: ASG scheduled the folk singer and balladeer Harry Chapin for two shows in Van Meter on 3 March 1974. Activities vice president Tom LaCivita called it the first example of his new concept of major-mini concerts, in which medium-priced performers were brought in, sometimes free and sometimes as a pay event.

events.title: Herald calls the lecture series ASG's best effort to date
events.body: The Herald judged ASG's 1973-74 lecture series its best effort yet. The series had carried Senator Barry Goldwater, former attorney general Elliot Richardson and Senator Edmund Muskie, and ASG jointly sponsored the psychic Uri Geller with the University Lecture Series.

events.title: Marshall Tucker Band is upstaged by Freddie King
events.body: ASG brought the Marshall Tucker Band to Diddle Arena on Monday 8 April 1974, with Freddie King leading in. The Talisman said King, brought back for encores by a screaming crowd, was the biggest crowd pleaser, while Diddle's acoustics destroyed much of Marshall Tucker's set and the disappointed crowd began drifting towards the doors halfway through.

events.title: Kool and the Gang announced to close the year
events.body: The Herald previewed boogie and bluegrass coming to campus, and the Talisman recorded that the soul show band Kool and the Gang was scheduled to close out ASG's year alongside a festival set for 27 April. Neither source confirms that either event took place.

events.title: Student-Faculty Interaction seminars
events.body: ASG set up a series of informative seminars under a Student-Faculty Interaction Program, run with the undergraduate advisement office. The programmes were informal meetings between students and department representatives to discuss possible majors, aimed at students who had not decided.

events.title: Steve Henry resigns the discount post
events.body: The Herald reported that Steve Henry had resigned his ASG discount post. Henry was elected ASG president a year later and ran on a platform of entertainment and student services.

events.title: Edmund Muskie calls for Nixon's impeachment in an ASG lecture
events.body: ASG sponsored the lecture Senator Edmund Muskie of Maine gave at Western on 11 December 1973, on the restoration of confidence in government. Muskie called for the impeachment of President Nixon, saying he had decided on the night of the Saturday Massacre that impeachment was the only way the issue should be raised. He cited a Harris poll in which 19 per cent of Americans said they had confidence in the executive branch. The 1974 Talisman lists Muskie with Barry Goldwater and Elliot Richardson among the lectures ASG sponsored that year.

src.label: 1974 Talisman, pp. 52-55 (Lectures); date from College Heights Herald 53:26, 4 Dec 1973

events.title: Sam Ervin analyses Watergate
events.body: Senator Sam Ervin, chairman of the Senate Watergate committee, spoke at Western on 2 April 1974 under a contract ASG had signed in February. The Herald reported the lecture on 5 April, and in the same issue judged ASG's 1973-74 lecture series its best effort to date.

leaders.name: Gregory McKinney
leaders.note: Student regent, not president. Sworn in 19 June 1974 as WKU's first African American student regent.

sources.label: WKU Timeline: Gregory McKinney (Western Alumnus, 19 Jun 1974)

profile: Gregory McKinney came to campus prominence as a speaker: in March 1974 the Herald reported him winning top honors in competition.

That spring McKinney ran for the student seat on the Board of Regents against Sid Stevens, the two candidates' final appeals running side by side in the Herald as an editorial called the race a clear choice for voters.
McKinney won the seat and was sworn in on June 19, 1974, becoming WKU's first African American student regent.

Midway through the fall 1974 semester, Herald writer Al Cross profiled the new regent under the headline 'Greg McKinney Feels Regents Can Aid Western's Progress,' as McKinney settled into his seat on the Board of Regents.
As the academic year closed, the Herald reported 'Student Regent Greg McKinney Calls Year Rewarding,' in the same issue that covered the regents approving a record budget and academic proposals.

After his term as student regent, McKinney stayed on at WKU as a graduate assistant in Student Affairs. The university's own file on him, opened in 1983, holds correspondence between McKinney and President Donald Zacharias and a paper he wrote titled "Student Affairs: An Analysis" - the record of a former student regent moving into the administration whose board he had once sat on.

leaders.name: Jeffrey Consolo
leaders.note: ASG president. The Herald of 1974 reports 'Jeff Consolo Tabs Eight for Congress' - a president making appointments to the Associated Student Congress.
profile: Jeff Consolo won the Associated Student Government presidency in the March 1974 election on a ticket with Steve Henry, in a cycle whose primary the Herald said showed Greek influence.
Taking office, Consolo told the Herald he hoped for increased student involvement during his term.

Consolo's term closed on April 15, 1975, when new ASG officers were installed at the day's meeting after a spring in which his congress had simplified election procedures and wound down its concert program.
Jeffrey Paul Consolo, of Mansfield, Ohio, served as the ninth president of WKU's Associated Student Government for the 1974-75 term, according to the SGA's own roster of former presidents.
Early in the fall 1974 semester, Consolo appointed eight students to seats in the ASG congress, reported by Jim Reynolds under the headline 'Jeff Consolo Tabs Eight for Congress.'

In early April 1975, as the polls prepared to open to elect his successor, the Herald ran 'Jeff Consolo Notes Progress in His Term' alongside items crediting ASG moves with cutting bookstore prices, gaining parking board input and folding the Volunteer Bureau into the organization.

events.title: Regents extend visitation as the year opens
events.body: The Herald's opening issue reported the Board of Regents extending dormitory visitation and approving a $29.8 million budget at the board's first session of the year.

events.title: Voting procedures simplified for the spring election
events.body: ASG passed a motion simplifying voting procedures for the spring election, and the ASG treasurer took to the Herald's letters column the same day.

events.title: New officers installed; concert plans dropped
events.body: New Associated Student Government officers were installed at the day's meeting, as the outgoing congress abandoned plans for a final concert of the semester and the editorial page pronounced incoming president Steve Henry's entertainment plan inadequate.

events.title: Keffer wins freshman vote; Consolo names eight to congress
events.body: The Herald reported that Jay Keffer won the freshman election for the top freshman post. In the same issue, ASG president Jeff Consolo tabbed eight students for seats in the ASG congress, and the Academic Council heard a proposal for more student votes.

events.title: Protesters urge ASG revamping
events.body: Protesters urged a revamping of the Associated Student Government. The same issue carried Janet Steen's report that ASG ecology projects were non-existent.

events.title: ASG schedules Kiss and initiates concert hour
events.body: ASG scheduled the rock band Kiss and initiated a concert hour, part of its role booking campus entertainment that fall. The concert program later became a major source of financial trouble for the organization.

events.title: Budget troubles threaten ASG entertainment role
events.body: The Herald reported that financial difficulties might force ASG to drop its entertainment duties, and the ASG congress heard the treasurer's budget explanation. Columnists Dave Allen and Craig Griffith examined the organization's budget problems in the same issue.

events.title: Quorum failures halt ASG twice in one week
events.body: ASG action was halted twice during the week by a lack of quorum. A Herald editorial said the confusion in ASG signaled a need for change.

events.title: Primary canceled; constitutional change approved
events.body: The primary election for Associated Student Government was canceled, and the student government approved a constitutional change. A letter writer in the same issue criticized the Herald's coverage of ASG.

events.title: Steve Henry elected to lead ASG
events.body: Following the spring election, the Herald reported that incoming president Steve Henry would give activities priority in Associated Student Government. The organization also prepared to name its top member, and the paper noted that Greeks continued to dominate the campus political scene.

events.title: Rain drives the Bluegrass Festival indoors
events.body: ASG sponsored a Bluegrass Festival on 28 August 1974, headlined by Lester Flatt and the Clinch Mountain Clan, who described their music as folk music with overdrive. Scheduled as an outdoor festival in the amphitheatre, it had to be moved into Van Meter Auditorium because of rain.

events.title: A $42,000 entertainment budget, $27,000 of it for two free concerts
events.body: ASG operated on a budget of $42,000 for all forms of entertainment in 1974-75. It set aside $27,000 for two free concerts and $15,000 for mini-concerts, dances and other acts, with major concerts financed by their own gate receipts.
events.money: $42,000 entertainment budget; $27,000 for two free concerts, $15,000 for mini-concerts and dances

events.title: Students picket the Doc Severinsen Homecoming concert
events.body: Doc Severinsen played the Homecoming concert on 11 October 1974 with Today's Children and the Now Generation Brass, before roughly 3,000 people, a substantial majority of them alumni. About thirty students picketed the doors; Severinsen complimented the audience for braving the picket lines and said he respected the demonstrators' right to exercise an American privilege.

events.title: Protest produces a coalition for change in concert booking
events.body: The Herald reported that the protest at the Severinsen concert had prompted a coalition seeking change in concert booking. The Student Action Committee that resulted argued that Ron Beck did not have the time the booking job needed and sought power for the activities vice president to negotiate with acts; Kentucky law prevented a student from controlling the funds, so the role stayed advisory, and the committee later folded into ASG's Student Activities Committee.

events.title: Barefoot Jerry costs ASG almost $1,500
events.body: The Nashville group Barefoot Jerry entertained a small crowd in Van Meter with a set that ranged across rock, country, blues and jazz and ended in a standing ovation. Activities vice president Tom LaCivita said ASG lost almost $1,500 on it; the Talisman, which does not date the show, called it one of the finer shows of its size at Western.

events.title: Al Stewart's mini-concert dies with his US tour
events.body: ASG booked Al Stewart for a mini-concert on 3 November 1974, but his United States tour was cancelled over immigration law. Tom LaCivita booked Kiss in his place, in an effort to ease the pressure students had put on ASG over its choice of acts.

events.title: America plays free and pushes ASG further into debt
events.body: ASG presented America as the first free concert of the school year on 7 November 1974, with Chad Stewart of Chad and Jeremy opening. Cracked speakers and feedback marred the sound, but lighters brought the band back for 'A Horse with No Name'; the Talisman recorded that ASG went into steadily increasing debt by presenting America free.

events.title: ASG establishes a service area
events.body: Jim Reynolds reported in the Herald that ASG had established a service area. The reorganisation of that year had put ASG's work into two areas, student affairs and academic affairs, with projects assigned to one or the other.

events.title: Kiss plays Van Meter and Ron Beck swears off the genre
events.body: Kiss played to a capacity crowd in Van Meter Auditorium on 7 December 1974, with smoke bombs, fire-eating, whiteface and leather bat wings, and Gene Simmons simulating vomiting and dripping stage blood over the front row. Ron Beck said afterwards that he would never again take part in booking this kind of act for Western because the show had no educational value for students.

events.title: War and the Charlie Daniels Band open warfare in Diddle
events.body: ASG's first major spring concert put War and the Charlie Daniels Band in Diddle Arena on 3 March 1975. Students called the Charlie Daniels set the best they had had in years and matches and lighters brought him back for 'Orange Blossom Special', but attendance was very low.

events.title: Bookstore prices cut and a part-time athletic discount approved
events.body: The Herald reported in the same issue that an ASG move had cut bookstore prices, that a part-time athletic discount had been approved and that the Volunteer Bureau had been made part of ASG. ASG had proposed raising the part-time incidental fee so part-time students could enter athletic events on the same footing as full-time students.

events.title: A better and cheaper student discount card
events.body: ASG changed the student discount card for what the Talisman described as a far better and cheaper one. The change was listed among the accomplishments of the Consolo administration alongside the new academic complaint system.

events.title: Pure Prairie League: sound ruins the first show, the second is far better
events.body: Associated Student Government billed Pure Prairie League, and the group played two shows in Van Meter on 31 January 1975. Sound problems ruined most of the first act at 7:30, and the bassist, printed in the Talisman as Mike Rieley, asked the 9:30 audience whether anyone had seen the first show. He said it was the group's first experience with the sound crew the university had contracted. The problems were solved before the second show, which the 1975 Talisman rated far better.

src.label: 1975 Talisman, Entertainment; announced in College Heights Herald 50:31, 24 Jan 1975

events.title: ASG books its fall entertainment fare
events.body: The Herald reported on 30 August 1974 that Associated Student Government had booked its entertainment programme for the fall semester. The 1975 Talisman set out the season that followed: an ASG bluegrass festival on 28 August, moved indoors to Van Meter Auditorium by rain and headlined by Lester Flatt and the Clinch Mountain Clan; Doc Severinsen at Homecoming on 11 October, picketed by about 30 students; and America free on 7 November. ASG had booked Al Stewart for a 3 November mini-concert, but his United States tour was cancelled over immigration law and activities vice-president Tom LaCivita booked Kiss in his place.

events.title: ASG broke even on the Bar-Kays mini-concert
events.body: The Herald of 25 October 1974 billed the Bar-Kays for a mini-concert that night. The 1975 Talisman records that ASG presented the seven-member group, the backing band on Isaac Hayes's 'Hot Buttered Soul' and 'Shaft' albums, as one of its major mini-concerts of the year, and that ASG broke even on the concert.

events.title: ASG took over the Student Volunteer Bureau and the tutorial programme
events.body: The Student Volunteer Bureau, which placed students in community volunteer work, weakened when founder Rodney Berry could not secure administrators or funds. Berry approached ASG president Jeff Consolo about folding it into ASG, and the Talisman recorded the merger passing at the last meeting of the fall semester by better than 80 per cent, with the tutorial programme consolidated into ASG at the same time. The Herald of 21 January 1975 reported that ASG had agreed to administer the bureau and had rescued it.

leaders.name: Steve Henry
leaders.note: Likely the Steve Henry who later served as Lieutenant Governor of Kentucky (1995-2003). Wikipedia's biography of Stephen L. Henry (b. 8 Oct 1953) states he was elected WKU Student Body President "in his second attempt, after losing a close election the preceding year to Jeff Costello," and served on the WKU Board of Regents as a Kentucky resident while president - matching this record's own Herald sourcing almost exactly: Jeffrey Consolo (not "Costello", likely a Wikipedia transcription of the same name) won the presidency in spring 1974, and the Herald's 30 Apr 1976 wrap-up of Henry's term specifically describes him balancing the dual jobs of student regent and ASG president. The match in name, university, era, and this specific narrative beat is treated as verification, but the identification rests on a secondary source (Wikipedia), not a WKU archive document that states it outright - flagged here rather than treated as fully closed.
profile: Steve Henry appeared in ASG coverage as early as September 1972, when the Herald reported his view that the Associated Student Government had lost respect.
Henry won the spring 1974 election on a ticket with Jeff Consolo, and resigned his post running the student discount program after the victory.

As president in 1975-76 Henry moved in November to change ASG's concert proposal after a money-losing fall season, while a student group urged support for his energy awareness plan. At year's end the Herald summed up his tenure with a piece on how the role had required balancing the twin jobs of student regent and ASG president, which he held at the same time.

A Wikipedia biography of Stephen L. Henry, later the 52nd Lieutenant Governor of Kentucky (1995-2003), describes an orthopedic surgeon and WKU alumnus who was elected Student Body President on his second attempt after an earlier loss, and who sat on the WKU Board of Regents as president - a career arc that lines up point for point with this record's own Herald sourcing, though no WKU archive document has yet been found that states the identification directly.

events.title: Big concert, big loss
events.body: An ASG concert drew 4,300 people but lost $7,000, the Herald reported, opening a money argument that ran through the fall.

events.title: ASG suggests a campus bank
events.body: ASG suggested creating a campus bank for students, one of the new administration's early service proposals.

events.title: Budget approved amid concert debate
events.body: The ASG budget won approval as concerts were discussed, two weeks after the money-losing season opener had put the program under scrutiny.

events.title: Fund misuse charges aired
events.body: Charges of ASG fund misuse were heard in the same week the congress voted to create an activities committee and a letter writer attacked the organization.

events.title: A budget remedy and a book exchange
events.body: The Herald weighed whether a new ASG budget offered a remedy, and reported a spring semester book exchange to be co-sponsored by ASG and Veterans on Campus. President Steve Henry moved to change the concert proposal the same week.

events.title: Petition drive seeks support
events.body: ASG sought student support with a petition and prepared to hear appeals over its concert policy as the fall semester closed.

events.title: Election season and an acquittal
events.body: During the spring election season ASG acquitted congress member Gerard Faulk in an internal proceeding, and the Herald polled voters on the races.

events.title: Final meeting approves a budget
events.body: The congress approved a tentative budget at the final ASG meeting of the year, and the Herald assessed how Steve Henry's year had required balancing his twin jobs as student regent and ASG president.

events.title: Faulk impeachment hearings open as campaign begins
events.body: The Associated Student Government began impeachment hearings against congress member Gerard Faulk the same week candidates for the spring election, including Christy Vogt, were set to speak to students. An editorial the same issue held up Associated Student Government's troubles as a cautionary example for the university's newly forming Faculty Senate.

events.title: Christy Vogt wins the ASG presidency
events.body: The Herald reported Christy Vogt's win in the Associated Student Government presidential election under the headline "Christy Vogt Wins Election," with Vogt's own "Winner Says Thanks" running in the same issue. The paper reported the result the same week Gerard Faulk was acquitted in his impeachment case.

events.title: Bruce Smith and Christy Vogt survive the primary, 527 ballots cast
events.body: The Herald reported the Associated Student Government presidential primary under the headline "Bruce Smith, Christy Vogt Survive as 527 Cast Ballots," the two advancing to the 9 April runoff that Vogt went on to win.

events.title: Herald supplement recaps a year of ASG wins
events.body: A special supplement to the Herald, paid for and written by the Associated Student Government, summed up the outgoing Henry administration's year: women's hours abolished with ASG's backing, better intramural facilities credited to ASG resolutions, a new ASG discount card program, a second campus site for cashing checks, and a Veterans on Campus book exchange. The supplement also printed the year's roster of congress members and its bills and resolutions, and carried Christy Vogt's own piece on laundry facility improvement.

events.title: Regents add $16,000 to the entertainment budget and buy a second free concert
events.body: The Board of Regents passed a $16,000 increase in the ASG entertainment budget in August 1975. President Steve Henry said the increase allowed a second free concert and that he had never known one year to have two free concerts, much less two in a semester.
events.money: $16,000 increase in the ASG entertainment budget

events.title: Gove, Alex Harvey and Bottom and Company welcome students back
events.body: Two free concerts opened the fall semester to welcome students back, featuring Gove, Alex Harvey and Bottom and Company at the fine arts centre outdoor theatre. Harvey picked a dulcimer with a feather during his set.

events.title: ASG sponsors LAMB, a messianic music duo
events.body: On 11 September 1975 ASG sponsored LAMB, a duo specialising in messianic music, in Van Meter Auditorium. The Talisman noted the concert was well attended, perhaps because many students had writing assignments for MC 272 classes that required it.

events.title: Loggins and Messina open the season and lose $7,000
events.body: Kenny Loggins and Jim Messina played the first major concert of the year in Diddle Arena on Wednesday 17 September 1975, with the Amazing Rhythm Aces also on the bill. The crowd of 4,300 was too small and ASG lost about $7,000; activities vice president Rick Kelley blamed a lack of student body support.

events.title: Jules Bergman speaks on '2000 A.D. - The Way it Will Be'
events.body: ABC science editor Jules Bergman came to campus on 23 September 1975 for the first guest of the University Lecture Series, which the Talisman notes was also sponsored by ASG. Poor weather hurt the crowd; Bergman said man was adaptable enough to fly to the moon six times but could not endure much longer what he had created for himself on earth.

events.title: Doug Kershaw takes three encores in Homecoming week
events.body: ASG brought the Cajun fiddler Doug Kershaw for the Thursday night of Homecoming week, 30 October 1975. About 700 people saw him jump into the crowd to lead 'Jambalaya' and land in the lap of a startled coed in the fourth row; he took three encores and closed with 'Louisiana Man'.

events.title: Pat Paulsen returns for a free 'Lecture in Humor'
events.body: Pat Paulsen entertained a Diddle Arena crowd on Homecoming eve, 31 October 1975, at a free show sponsored by ASG. Presenting 'A Lecture in Humor', he traced the history of comedy from prehistoric times to the future and said he had found out you cannot speak your mind and expect to get elected.

events.title: ASG creates a student activities committee for concerts, lectures and publicity
events.body: To settle the dispute over booking, ASG adopted a Student Activities Committee, put into operation on 2 December 1975 and chaired by Rick Kelley. From 63 applicants, 17 members were chosen across three subcommittees, seven for concerts, five for lectures and five for publicity, each with alternates.

events.title: Oliver and Jerico Harp play free to a sparse crowd
events.body: A sparse crowd attended the Oliver and Jerico Harp concert on Wednesday 3 December 1975. The Talisman described it as a freebie to students.

events.title: ASG and Veterans on Campus run a book exchange against the bookstore
events.body: To give students an alternative to the College Heights Bookstore, ASG co-sponsored a book exchange with Veterans on Campus from 12 to 26 January 1976. Administrative vice president Christy Vogt said the two groups had covered expenses by 21 January through the sale of over 600 books, with ASG and VOC making 25 cents on each book sold.
events.money: over 600 books sold; 25 cents profit per book

events.title: A second campus check-cashing facility opens after an ASG survey
events.body: An ASG survey at fall registration found that the most significant desire of students was a new check-cashing facility. A second campus check-cashing point opened in the customer service area of the bookstore on 26 January 1976 for nine hours a week, after the original proposal for a full-service campus bank branch was judged impractical by area bankers.

events.title: George Allen lectures on success and ambition
events.body: George Allen, head coach of the Washington Redskins, spoke in the Garrett Conference Center on 12 February 1976 in one of the spring ASG-sponsored lectures. He showed a film, answered questions on professional football and advised those facing a tight job market that the last thing to talk about when looking for a job is money.

events.title: Chris Miller of National Lampoon draws 1,100 and a rebuke from the dean
events.body: Chris Miller of National Lampoon drew about 1,100 people to the Garrett Conference Center on 24 February 1976 with a lecture titled 'Toe Sucking in Albania, or An Evening of Erotic Laughter'. Three days later the Herald reported that dean of student affairs Charles Keown had criticised ASG's taste in sponsoring the lecture.

events.title: George Wallace is fought over in committee and never appears
events.body: President Steve Henry reported a 99 per cent chance of getting George Wallace, then seeking the Democratic presidential nomination, to speak in April 1976. A subcommittee of ASG's Student Activities Committee voted 4-2 with one abstention on 6 February to strike Wallace from the list of lecturers on the grounds that the arrangements had been made improperly, ASG Congress overruled the resolution, and by 13 February the Herald reported the lecture was uncertain; no appearance is recorded.

events.title: Truman Capote lectures off the cuff
events.body: Truman Capote lectured on 21 April 1976. The Herald's account two days later reported that off-the-cuff remarks were the highlight.

events.title: ASG plans an activities grand finale
events.body: The Herald reported that ASG was planning an activities grand finale to end the year. The fortnight that followed carried the Truman Capote lecture, two teacher forums and the free James Taylor concert.

events.title: ASG to sponsor two teacher forums
events.body: The Herald reported that ASG would sponsor two teacher forums. They came at the end of a year in which ASG had also pushed through the academic complaint system.

events.title: ASG's own supplement counts the discount cards and the book exchange
events.body: In the Student Insight supplement it paid for and wrote itself, ASG set out its services for the year: the discount cards it sponsored, the book exchange run with Veterans on Campus which it called a success, and its work on laundry facilities and intramural facilities. Christy Vogt wrote the piece on laundry improvements and Elaine Boeckman the piece on the abolition of women's hours.

events.title: Laundry improvements take effect
events.body: From 15 April 1976 the university installed more washers and dryers, an air-conditioned study area and a laundry pick-up service, with dry cleaning by a local firm in the proposal. Steve Henry said he hoped the facilities, which ASG had proposed the previous October, would be long-lasting.

events.title: ASG sets up a Student Activities Committee to choose the acts
events.body: After a semester of argument over who should decide what came to campus, ASG adopted a Student Activities Committee to bring more student opinion into the booking and publicising of concerts and lecturers. Seventeen members were chosen from 63 applicants and divided into concert, lecture and publicity sub-committees, with alternates for each. The dispute behind it had begun when an assistant dean of student affairs argued that any programme the university presented ought to have educational value; students wrote to the Herald against him.

events.title: Linda Ronstadt's Homecoming concert nets ASG $4,300
events.body: Linda Ronstadt played the Homecoming concert in Diddle Arena on Saturday 1 November 1975, opening with "Colorado", with Goose Creek Symphony before her and Andrew Gold as her backup group. The 1976 Talisman put the crowd at about 6,500 and the profit to ASG at $4,300, and reported that activities vice-president Rick Kelley and ASG president Steve Henry rated it among the most successful concerts in years - successful enough, the yearbook said, to guarantee a free Spinners and Wet Willie concert for students on 30 January.
events.money: netted $4,300 for ASG; attendance about 6,500, though the same yearbook's opening section gives 6,300

events.title: James Taylor plays a free concert to close the year
events.body: The Herald of 20 April 1976 billed James Taylor for a free concert that Friday, and the issue of 23 April told readers the performance would be that night. The next issue, 27 April, carried Tip Shanklin's review under the headline "Evening with James Taylor Well Spent", so the concert took place. The 1976 Talisman listed James Taylor among the year's concerts but, before the event, recorded only that he was scheduled to give a free concert in April.

events.title: ASG sponsored Natalie Cole in Van Meter
events.body: The Herald reported on 9 December 1975 that Associated Student Government would sponsor a concert by the jazz vocalist Natalie Cole. The 1976 Talisman records that Cole, daughter of the late Nat King Cole, performed in Van Meter Auditorium on 10 December to an estimated crowd of 325, singing 'This Will Be', 'Killing Me Softly With His Song', 'Honky Tonk Women' and 'You Are the Sunshine of My Life'.

events.title: Charles Berlitz opens the ASG lecture series on the Bermuda Triangle
events.body: Charles Berlitz, author of The Bermuda Triangle, opened the Associated Student Government lecture series in Van Meter Auditorium on 9 September 1975. The Herald carried the advance notice that morning; the 1976 Talisman reported a standing-room-only audience and recorded that Berlitz said more than 100 planes and ships and 1,000 people had vanished in the region since 1945, and that he ran through theories from heavy magnetisation to alien beings.

events.title: The Spinners and Wet Willie drew 7,500 to a free concert
events.body: The Spinners and Wet Willie played free to students on 30 January 1976 before a crowd of 7,500, the second straight major ASG promotion to make money. It was the first concert the new Student Activities Committee helped bring about. The Spinners worked impressions of the Ink Spots, the Mills Brothers, Tom Jones, the Miracles and Elvis Presley into the set, donned wigs for the Supremes, and came back for two encores.

leaders.name: Christy Mollozzi
leaders.note: The Herald's 9 April 1976 headline "Christy Vogt Wins Election" and her own "Winner Says Thanks" the same issue confirm the 1976-77 ASG presidency was won under the name Christy Vogt; her byline runs through the term (campaign endorsement 26 Mar 1976, "Urges Involvement" 12 Apr 1977, the closing letter to Congress 26 Apr 1977). The plaque records her as Christy Mollozzi. WKU's own archive ties the two names together in multiple places written by the university itself, not by this project: a WKU Archives research notecard indexed as "Mollozzi, Christy Vogt," and Christy Mollozzi appearing in the President's Office finding aids for the Meredith and Ransdell administrations in connection with Marketing & Promotions, meaning she had a further career on the WKU staff. "Christy Vogt Mollozzi" follows the ordinary American convention of a married name with the maiden name kept as a middle name. No single source states outright "formerly Christy Vogt," so this is an inference from a consistent name pattern repeated across independent WKU records over three decades, not a documented fact - flagged here rather than asserted as certain.

sources.label: UA37/30/2 WKU Research Notecards-Sources ("Mollozzi, Christy Vogt")

profile: Christy Vogt entered the spring 1976 Associated Student Government campaign with an endorsement from Herald columnist John Butchko, in an issue whose front section also covered the start of impeachment hearings against congress member Gerard Faulk and an editorial warning the university's new Faculty Senate away from ASG's own troubles.

Vogt and Bruce Smith survived the 2 April primary as the Herald reported 527 ballots cast, then Vogt won the presidency outright, the paper reporting the result on 9 April 1976 under the headline "Christy Vogt Wins Election," with her own note of thanks to voters in the same issue - the same week Faulk was acquitted.

In office for 1976-77, Vogt's congress created a constitutional revision committee within its first month (Bill 2, 7 September 1976) and kept revision on its agenda all year. It asked the university for a minimum wage policy for student employees (Resolution, 26 October 1976), recommended preregistration for all students, and opposed a proposed tuition increase (Bill 9, 8 March 1977) while creating a Complaint Committee to field student grievances the same meeting. A resolution on discrimination failed in February 1977 with fourteen members abstaining. The fall Seals and Crofts concert lost the organization $3,800, a recurring sore point ASG had wrestled with under Vogt's predecessors as well.

Vogt wrote her own case for the office in the Herald - "Urges Involvement," 12 April 1977, days before Bob Moore won the presidency to succeed her by a 26-vote margin. She closed her term on 26 April 1977 with a letter to Congress thanking its members and recommending four items to the administration: constitutional revision, extended hours for student buildings, open visitation, and advance registration - the same four causes her congress had pushed all year.

WKU's own archive later indexes her, alongside her maiden name, as Christy Vogt Mollozzi, and separately as Christy Mollozzi in President's Office records tied to Marketing & Promotions - evidence, though not a documented statement, that she went on to a career on the university's own staff.

events.title: Bob Moore elected ASG president by 26 votes
events.body: One of the narrowest margins in the record. The same issue carries the outgoing president congratulating voters, the faculty asking for a say in hiring, and Western fighting a beer licence for a local pizzeria.

events.title: Four candidates open the race to succeed Vogt
events.body: The Herald previewed a crowded ASG election: Tom Blair, Kirt Grubbs, Mark McChesney and Bob Moore all sought the presidency, with voting set for a Tuesday primary. Three candidates ran for the administrative vice presidency and four for the activities post in the same election.

events.title: ASG creates constitutional revision committee
events.body: The Associated Student Government congress passed Bill 2, creating a committee charged with revising the organization's constitution. Constitutional revision remained on the ASG agenda for the rest of the school year and appeared again among proposed amendments and a spring referendum bill.

src.label: SGA Records (UA66), Bill 2 - Constitutional Revision Committee, 7 Sep 1976

events.title: ASG asks WKU for a student minimum wage
events.body: The congress adopted Resolution 13, proposing that Western institute a minimum wage policy for all student employees. It was part of a heavy fall docket that also included resolutions on parking, laundry services, non-smoking areas and residence hall change machines.

src.label: SGA Records (UA66), Resolution 13 - Minimum Wage, 26 Oct 1976

events.title: Seals and Crofts concert loses ASG $3,800
events.body: The Herald reported that the Seals and Crofts concert set the Associated Student Government back $3,800. Concert finances would remain a recurring sore point for ASG through the rest of the decade.

events.title: ASG recommends preregistration for all students
events.body: The Herald reported that ASG would recommend preregistration for all students. Advance registration was one of the four items president Christy Vogt later carried into her end-of-year recommendations to the administration.

events.title: Discrimination resolution fails as 14 abstain
events.body: Fourteen members abstained as the Associated Student Government rejected a resolution on discrimination, the Herald reported. The same issue noted that filing for ASG posts would begin the following Monday.

events.title: Bill calls for ASG to evaluate itself
events.body: Bill 6 proposed that the Associated Student Government conduct a self-evaluation "for the purposes of transparency and improvement."

src.label: SGA Records (UA66), Bill 6 - ASG Evaluation, 15 Feb 1977

events.title: ASG passes bill opposing tuition increase
events.body: The congress approved Bill 9, formally opposing a proposed tuition increase. The same March meeting produced Bill 8, which created a Complaint Committee to handle student grievances.

src.label: SGA Records (UA66), Bill 9 - Opposition to Tuition Increase, 8 Mar 1977

events.title: Vogt closes the congress with four recommendations
events.body: President Christy Vogt sent a letter closing the congress and thanking ASG members for their work. She left four items to recommend to the administration: constitutional revision, extended hours for student buildings, open visitation and advanced registration.

src.label: SGA Records (UA66), Christy Vogt Letter, 26 Apr 1977

events.title: Vogt urges involvement as her term closes
events.body: With her term nearly over, president Christy Vogt wrote "Urges Involvement" for the Herald, days before Bob Moore's election to succeed her.

events.title: ASG and the Center Board publish the 1976-77 events schedule
events.body: The summer Herald carried the University Center Board and ASG schedule of events for 1976-77. By late August the Herald was reporting two lectures and two concerts on ASG's entertainment slate and that ASG was seeking an appearance by Chicago.

events.title: Lori Wolfson opens the mini-concert series
events.body: ASG continued its mini-concert series with the acoustic guitarist Lori Wolfson in Van Meter Auditorium on 10 September 1976. The second, on 22 September, was Jerico Harp, whose Jim Thomas and Tom Schmidt mixed their own material with songs including Dan Fogelberg's 'Wysteria'.

events.title: 400 books sold in the ASG and Veterans on Campus co-op
events.body: The Herald reported that 400 books had been sold in the book co-op ASG ran with Veterans on Campus. The exchange had been advertised in the first issue of the year.

events.title: Students petition for their Maranatha concert money back
events.body: Students petitioned ASG for the return of a concert payment connected with the Maranatha Christian Center. ASG voted to refund the Maranatha money on 1 October, and by 8 October the Herald reported the Judicial Council had dropped the ASG-Maranatha case.

events.title: Bob Woodward cancels and comes six months late
events.body: Carl Bernstein was booked to open the lecture season but contracted pneumonia, and his partner Bob Woodward was announced as a substitute before cancelling his Western and University of Kentucky dates for work. Promoters paid the advertising costs for the cancelled lecture, but someone in the ASG office drew a bull's-eye on Woodward's publicity poster; he finally appeared in early April 1977.

events.title: Chicago grosses $53,092 and becomes Western's most successful concert
events.body: Chicago appeared at Diddle Arena on 15 October 1976, drew 10,450 people and grossed $53,092. The 1977 Talisman called it Western's most financially successful concert. The show cost $25,000 and was promoted by Reggae Ltd of St Louis with ASG, the first privately promoted concert at Western; about 5,000 advance tickets were sold, another record, and Ron Beck called it one of the best the university had ever had.

events.title: Seals and Crofts play Homecoming and lose $3,800
events.body: Jim Seals and Dash Crofts returned to Western for the Homecoming concert on Saturday 6 November 1976, with the Cate Brothers opening. About 5,200 attended and the concert lost roughly $3,800; Ron Beck blamed the Saturday date, saying everyone was worn out from the rest of Homecoming day. Afterwards the pair held a fireside chat with about 80 students about their Baha'i faith.

events.title: ASG Homecoming dance with the Back Stabbers and Those Perfections
events.body: For those who wanted livelier Homecoming entertainment, ASG sponsored a dance in the Garrett Conference Center Ballroom featuring the Back Stabbers and Those Perfections. It ran the same weekend as the Seals and Crofts concert.

events.title: Barry Manilow plays free to 7,000 and cuts his set short
events.body: Barry Manilow gave the only free major concert of the semester on Monday 15 November 1976 before 7,000 people. The show cost $23,000, with ticket sales subtracting $10,100 from that; a heckler on the first row put Manilow in a bad mood, so he dropped his commercial set and cut the show by fifteen minutes.
events.money: cost $23,000, less $10,100 in ticket sales; attendance 7,000

events.title: Clive Barnes, John Sears and Vincent Bugliosi on the lecture series
events.body: The lecture season carried Clive Barnes of the New York Times in early November on 'The Plight of the Theatre Today', John Sears, Nixon's 1968 campaign manager and later Reagan's, in late November, and Vincent Bugliosi, the Manson prosecutor and author of 'Helter Skelter', in early December. Members of the ASG lecture committee, David Carwell, Ricky Sheppard and Mike Seiler, hosted the visiting speakers.

events.title: David Frye fills Van Meter with impersonations of Nixon
events.body: The comedian David Frye kept a capacity crowd in Van Meter Hall laughing in mid-September 1976 with impersonations of political figures and film stars, Richard Nixon foremost among them. In January the comedian Robert Klein warmed about 700 people in the Garrett Conference Center ballroom in arctic weather.

events.title: ASG considers cutting off the Volunteer Bureau
events.body: The Herald reported that ASG might discontinue funding for the Student Volunteer Bureau. A week later an editorial argued the bureau should have ASG's support; ASG kept funding it for another year before stopping in May 1978.

events.title: Book exchange sells more than 1,100 books
events.body: The Herald reported that the book exchange had sold more than 1,100 books. It was the strongest showing yet for the co-op ASG ran with Veterans on Campus.

events.title: Ethos returns for a Valentine's Day mini-concert
events.body: Ethos appeared on Valentine's Day 1977 in ASG's mini-concert series. The band had first played Western as an ASG mini-concert in October 1973.

events.title: Rufus and Wild Cherry draw 6,500 to a loud spring show
events.body: Rufus and Wild Cherry headlined the first major spring concert on 23 March 1977, opened by Fresh, whom Ron Beck signed for $500 because they were a favourite of Wild Cherry. About 6,500 attended, roughly 4,000 of them students, and Chaka Khan sang on her birthday; Beck said students told him the concert was too loud and that Rufus did not perform to their expectations.
events.money: attendance about 6,500; opening act Fresh cost $500

events.title: Student discount card covers 29 merchants
events.body: The Herald reported that the student discount card offered reductions from 29 merchants. The same issue carried Rick Kelley's review of a year in which Chicago and Barry Manilow headlined the concerts and a prosecutor and a reporter were among the speakers.

events.title: Jimmy Buffett and the Coral Reefer Band closed the concert year
events.body: The Herald announced on 25 March 1977 that a Jimmy Buffett concert was set for 27 April. The 1977 Talisman records that Buffett and the Coral Reefer Band played Diddle Arena that night, drawing three encores after a ninety-minute set from a small crowd, with highlights from 'Changes in Latitudes, Changes in Attitudes' and tunes from 'Livin' and Dyin' in 3/4 Time', 'A-1-A' and 'Havana Daydreamin''. The concert lost money, and the yearbook counts Buffett among the acts brought to Western in 1976-77 by the ASG concert programme run by activities vice president Rick Kelley.

leaders.name: Robert Moore
leaders.note: Elected ASG president by a 26-vote margin, reported 15 April 1977. Herald bylines call him 'Bob Moore.'
profile: Moore was one of four candidates - with Tom Blair, Kirt Grubbs and Mark McChesney - who opened the 1977 Associated Student Government presidential race on April 1. Moore and Blair survived the primary into the general election; McChesney did not, and by April 12 his letter backing Moore ran in the Herald alongside endorsements for the rest of the ticket, as outgoing president Christy Vogt urged students to get involved. The Herald's April 8 issue had set up the contest alongside the treasurer's race between George Carlson and rivals.

Moore won on April 15, 1977, by 26 votes over Blair - one of the narrowest presidential margins in the record - in an issue that also carried the faculty asking for a say in hiring and Western fighting a beer licence for a local pizzeria.

That October, as president, Moore publicly questioned how freshman candidates in that fall's class elections were spending their campaign money. The comment drew enough pushback that the Herald ran an editorial the same week headlined 'Bob Moore's Comment Isn't Good Politics.'

The archive does not yet show what Moore's administration did over the winter and into the spring beyond the ordinary business of readying his succession - see the 1978 election events below. By September 1978, after his term had ended, the Herald reported that Moore had been found ineligible for another Associated Student Government job; the archive does not yet hold the article's account of why.

events.title: Spending limits set for the coming ASG election
events.body: The Associated Student Government set spending limits for candidates ahead of the spring election that would choose Moore's successor.

events.title: Thornton and Johnson contest the presidency; four offices go uncontested
events.body: Steve Thornton and Ed Johnson faced off for the Associated Student Government presidency, Thornton campaigning on his experience, while four other offices had no opponent on the ballot.

events.title: Johnson contests his loss to Thornton
events.body: Ed Johnson, having lost the presidential race, contested the Associated Student Government election result.

events.title: ASG awaits approval of constitution changes
events.body: The Herald reported that the Associated Student Government was awaiting approval of changes to its constitution as the fall term opened. The story ran alongside a look at how ASG's concert booking process actually worked.

events.title: David Bass named ASG vice president
events.body: The Associated Student Government named David Bass its new vice president. The same issue carried Moore's letter disputing the Herald's editorial on candidate spending.

events.title: ASG and Interhall Council back coed dorm, end of door-ajar rule
events.body: ASG and the Interhall Council backed a coed dorm and abolition of the door-ajar visitation rule. The vote followed weeks in which the two bodies weighed a dorm petition and the Herald urged ASG to represent students in the dorm protest.

events.title: ASG signs Atlanta Rhythm Section and Brick
events.body: ASG signed Atlanta Rhythm Section and Brick for spring concerts. Ticket sales proved weak, and by late February the Herald was reporting on the organization's concert losses.

events.title: Concert losses will not stop a free concert
events.body: The Herald reported that losses would not halt an ASG free concert, and that ASG had thrown in towels as a bonus for performers. An editorial declared that the cry for better concerts had finally been heard.

events.title: ASG elections held with four offices uncontested
events.body: Students voted in the Associated Student Government elections with four offices uncontested. Candidate Steve Thornton told the Herald his experience was an important factor in the race.

events.title: ASG books its first show of the year
events.body: The Herald reported in the first issue of the year that ASG had booked its first show. The same freshman issue advertised a used book exchange scheduled in West Hall.

events.title: Waylon Jennings plays after a cocaine arrest scare
events.body: Waylon Jennings and Jessi Colter opened the concert year on 9 September 1977 before about 5,000 people. Jennings and his secretary had been arrested in Nashville on a charge of conspiring to possess cocaine and some feared the show would be cancelled, but he was permitted to keep the date; Colter opened with a thirty-minute set before the band Waylon took over.

events.title: ASG proposes a campus shuttle bus
events.body: An ASG proposal said a shuttle bus was needed to relieve crowded parking lots. The Herald had editorialised a month earlier that a shuttle bus was the best answer to the parking problem.

events.title: Charlie Daniels rescues Homecoming after the Atlanta Rhythm Section cancels
events.body: The Atlanta Rhythm Section cancelled its Homecoming concert, and the Charlie Daniels Band came to Western's rescue on Homecoming eve, Thursday 27 October 1977. Daniels was promoting 'Midnight Wind' and played 'Long-Haired Country Boy', 'The South's Gonna Do It Again' and 'Orange Blossom Special'; ARS rescheduled for February.

events.title: Celebrity Ball plays the ASG Homecoming dance
events.body: Celebrity Ball, a rock group from Atlanta, entertained at an ASG-sponsored dance in the Garrett Conference Ballroom on Homecoming night, after the 20-20 tie with Morehead before an estimated 19,750 fans. It was the fiftieth Homecoming since Henry Hardin Cherry conceived the tradition in 1927.

events.title: Dave Mason and Kenny Loggins lose $13,200
events.body: Only 2,916 came to see Dave Mason and Kenny Loggins in Diddle Arena on 8 November 1977, a concert that cost the university about $31,200. The Herald reported a loss of $13,200; both men were riding new gold albums, Mason took one encore and Loggins three, and the shortfall nearly eliminated the free spring concert.

events.title: The book swap is called off for the spring
events.body: The Herald reported that the book swap was off for the spring semester. The same issue carried ASG's plans for its spring activities and a bill to support a state landlord-tenant measure.

events.title: Few tickets sold for the Atlanta Rhythm Section
events.body: The Herald reported that few tickets had been sold for the ASG concert by the Atlanta Rhythm Section. The warning proved accurate a week later.

events.title: Atlanta Rhythm Section and Brick lose $12,000 on Valentine's Day
events.body: The Atlanta Rhythm Section finally appeared on 14 February 1978, bringing fellow Atlantans Brick, who opened with 'Dazz' and 'Dusic'. Most of the audience left before ARS took the stage; only 2,346 tickets were sold and the university lost about $12,000. United Black Students had announced in January that it would help arrange for Brick and LTD to appear, but LTD did not.

events.title: Average White Band signed for the free concert
events.body: The Herald reported that groups had been signed for the free ASG concert, with the Average White Band on the bill. ASG had said in February that its losses would not halt the free concert.

events.title: Average White Band and the Ramsey Lewis Trio close the year free, and draw 3,300
events.body: The free spring concert on 18 April 1978 put the Average White Band and the Ramsey Lewis Trio in Diddle Arena and drew about 3,300, ASG's last show of the year. The Scottish group charged $10,000 and the talent fee for the Ramsey Lewis Trio was $5,000; the Herald's reviewer wrote that the band made a concerted effort but the fans were few.
events.money: AWB fee $10,000; Ramsey Lewis Trio fee $5,000; attendance about 3,300

events.title: Grandpa Jones and Lester Flatt at the Bluegrass Festival
events.body: Grandpa Jones entertained a crowd at the fine arts center amphitheatre during an ASG-sponsored Bluegrass Festival in the spring of 1978, with the Pinnacle Boys and Lester Flatt and the Nashville Grass also on the programme. The Herald reported on 25 April that the bluegrass crowds were relaxed and casual.

events.title: $23,000 of losses nearly cost ASG the concert programme
events.body: After ASG lost more than $23,000 on major concerts across the year, dean of student affairs Charles Keown recommended to the Board of Regents that its entertainment budget be halved for 1978-79 and that a committee study whether the University Center Board should take over programming. Bob Moore argued at the 29 April meeting that students would have less involvement if the change were made, and the regents voted to let ASG keep its full $62,000 entertainment budget while directing President Downing to appoint the study committee.
events.money: more than $23,000 lost on major concerts; $62,000 entertainment budget retained for 1978-79

events.title: ASG stops funding the Volunteer Bureau and starts a newsletter
events.body: The Herald reported that ASG had stopped funding the Student Volunteer Bureau and would start a newsletter. The bureau, which placed students in community volunteer work and in elementary school tutoring, had been part of ASG since January 1975.

events.title: Judicial Council denied Ed Johnson's election appeal
events.body: Losing candidate Ed Johnson contested the election result, and after a long debate the Associated Student Government Judicial Council denied his appeal. The ruling let Steve Thornton's win stand. While the case was pending the Herald had criticized the appeal system for a lack of objectivity.

events.title: Moore questioned freshman campaign spending and the Herald answered him
events.body: President Bob Moore publicly questioned how freshman class candidates were spending their campaign money, in a story the Herald headlined "A$G?". The paper answered the same week with an editorial arguing that Moore's comment was not good politics. Moore wrote back disputing the editorial.

leaders.name: Steven Thornton
leaders.note: Contested the ASG presidency against Ed Johnson in the 6 April 1978 election, campaigning on his experience; Johnson's contest of the result was denied by the Judicial Council on 18 April 1978 (see 1977-78 events, the outgoing Moore administration's year). This replaces a prior citation to 'Herald 54:54, 12 Apr 1979' - that issue is the following year's primary, does not name Thornton, and has been moved to 1979-80.
profile: Thornton beat Ed Johnson for the Associated Student Government presidency in the 6 April 1978 election, campaigning on his experience; Johnson contested the result, and the ASG Judicial Council denied his appeal on 18 April 1978 after a long debate.

In office that fall, Thornton's ASG tabled an open house bill rather than act on it, the Herald reported on 28 September 1978. By January 1979 the government faced a fight to keep control of student activities funding and was pressing for a student seat on a state-level council, both reported in the same 25 January 1979 issue.

In March 1979 the Herald reported Thornton and fellow WKU student Terri Craig elected to the executive council of the Student Government Association of Kentucky, a state-level body - the kind of state seat ASG had been pressing for two months earlier. In the last full week of his term, Thornton's ASG approved resolutions on campus housing and parking policy, reported 26 April 1979, the same week voting closed in the election for his successor. The archive does not otherwise show how the January activities-funding fight was resolved, and no further Herald coverage of the Thornton administration has been found before his successor, Jamie Hargrove, was profiled as the new ASG head at the start of the 1979-80 year.

events.title: President Dero Downing announces his resignation
events.body: Downing, who had led WKU since 1969, announced he would step down effective 31 December 1978. Vice President John Minton took over as interim president the following January while the Board of Regents searched for a successor.

events.title: ASG tables an open house bill
events.body: The Associated Student Government set aside a proposed open house bill rather than act on it, one of the fall semester's first pieces of business under new president Steven Thornton.

events.title: John Minton sworn in as interim president
events.body: Vice President John Minton was sworn in as WKU's interim president by Judge Charles Reynolds, succeeding Dero Downing and holding the post until Donald Zacharias took office that August.

events.title: ASG signs three lectures for the spring
events.body: The Associated Student Government signed three lectures for the spring semester, part of its ongoing role booking campus speakers.

events.title: ASG could lose control of activities funding
events.body: The Associated Student Government faced losing control over student activities funding, the Herald reported, a direct threat to one of the government's core powers.

events.title: ASG wants a student on a state council
events.body: In the same issue that reported the funding fight, the Associated Student Government pressed for a student seat on a state-level council, part of the broader campaign for student representation that ran through the decade.

events.title: Thornton and Craig win seats on Kentucky's student government council
events.body: The Herald reported two Western students, ASG president Steven Thornton and Terri Craig, elected to the executive council of the Student Government Association of Kentucky, a state-level student body - the kind of state seat ASG had pressed for in January.

events.title: Voting held for Thornton's successor; United Black Students backs Hargrove
events.body: Students voted in the Associated Student Government presidential election, with the Herald running candidate endorsements the same day, including United Black Students' backing of Jamie Hargrove.

events.title: ASG approves resolutions on housing and parking policy
events.body: In one of the outgoing Thornton administration's final acts, the Associated Student Government approved resolutions addressing campus housing and parking policy.

events.title: Roll-call votes made public; Moore ruled ineligible
events.body: ASG decided its roll-call votes would be made public, the Herald reported. The same issue reported that former president Bob Moore was ineligible for an Associated Student Government job.

events.title: David Rue wins freshman presidency by 11 votes
events.body: In the freshman election held under ASG, David Rue was elected president by 11 votes. Only 95 students had voted in the freshman primary the week before.

events.title: ASG backs Thornton's plan for minority representation
events.body: The Associated Student Government backed president Steve Thornton's plan to add minorities to the regents' presidential screening panel. The Herald's editorial page argued the regents should appoint a minority representative.

events.title: ASG approves revised constitution
events.body: The congress approved a revised Associated Student Government constitution. The revision capped a fall in which ASG also pushed teacher evaluations and parking rezoning.

events.title: ASG establishes a Minorities Board
events.body: ASG established a Minorities Board, the Herald reported. The move followed the fall's push to add minority voices to the presidential screening process.

events.title: Thornton and Craig elected to SGAK executive council
events.body: Two Western students, Steve Thornton and Terri Craig, were elected to the Student Government Association of Kentucky executive council. The Herald also editorialized that ASG should make its teacher evaluation public.

events.title: Election day: candidates lean on experience
events.body: Students voted in the ASG general election, with the presidential candidates relying on their experience, the Herald reported. United Black Students backed Jamie Hargrove, and outgoing president Steve Thornton and former president Bob Moore published endorsements.

events.title: Jamie Hargrove easily wins the presidency
events.body: The Herald reported that Jamie Hargrove easily won the Associated Student Government president race. The result closed an election season that had begun with 70 candidates signing up for offices.

events.title: ASG hands its concerts to an outside promoter
events.body: The Board of Regents gave ASG authority to seek outside help booking concerts, and ASG contracted Sunshine Promotions of Indianapolis, producers of a Rolling Stones show in Lexington that summer and of Summer Jam II in Louisville. The firm had booked more than 150 concerts; for its part of the bargain ASG was to receive 13 percent of the net profits. President Steve Thornton said at least three major concerts were being planned for the year.
events.money: ASG to take 13 percent of net profits

src.label: College Heights Herald, Vol. 54, No. 5, 7 September 1978

events.title: Player and Exile play the Homecoming concert
events.body: Player and Exile played Diddle Arena on Homecoming night to 4,296 people. Player, whose hits were "This Time I'm In It For Love" and "Baby Come Back," failed to get the crowd on its feet; Exile, from Richmond, skipped its sound check and played through poor sound but had the arena standing. After $24,000 in production costs and Western's 13 percent cut of a $25,694.29 after-tax gross, the Talisman recorded that there was little financial success to speak of.
events.money: $25,694.29 after-tax gross; $24,000 production costs; Western took 13 percent

events.title: The Herald tells ASG to quit the concert business
events.body: An unsigned Herald editorial said it was time ASG got out of the concert business, arguing that concert promotion had taken most of the organisation's time and effort and that ASG could not even hire a promoter competently. It cited excessive university demands, poor communication with Sunshine Promotions and the unsigned contract behind the Homecoming show. The same issue carried a reader's letter defending the concert as good.

src.label: College Heights Herald, Vol. 54, No. 23, 9 November 1978

events.title: Joe Cocker drops out; Wet Willie takes his place
events.body: Joe Cocker, who had been announced to appear with the Outlaws at Diddle Arena on 5 December, cancelled his entire tour, and Sunshine Promotions signed the southern rock band Wet Willie in his place. Advertisements in that issue read "ASG and WKU Present" the Outlaws with special guest Wet Willie, 7:30 p.m., $6 in advance and $7 on the day of the show. The same meeting heard that Eleanor Smeal, president of the National Organization for Women, would speak on 7 December in Van Meter Auditorium.

src.label: College Heights Herald, Vol. 54, No. 27, 28 November 1978

events.title: The Outlaws cancel after 242 tickets sell
events.body: Reaction to the advertising for the Outlaws and Wet Willie was so poor that only 242 tickets had been sold by the week of the show. When the Outlaws' manager heard the figure he cancelled on the spot, according to university programs coordinator Tim Nemeth. The December date, ASG's replacement for the Joe Cocker booking, never happened.

events.title: John Prine sells out Van Meter and ASG still loses $2,000
events.body: John Prine came to Western in the autumn of 1978 and did what no other musical act had done in a long time, playing to a capacity house. But Van Meter Auditorium holds only slightly more than 1,000, and even with a sellout and tickets priced higher than any previous mini-concert, ASG lost about $2,000 on the show. His five-man band ran through 25 songs, among them "Spanish Pipedream," "Dear Abby," "The Bottomless Lake" and "Sam Stone."

events.title: Eleanor Smeal's lecture keeps slipping
events.body: Activities vice president David Carwell told ASG's first meeting of the semester that the university was still trying to reschedule a lecture by Eleanor Smeal, president of the National Organization for Women, for February or March; she had been announced for 7 December and had not come. He set out what ASG was paying the three speakers it had signed: $4,000 for Dick Gregory, $2,000 for Princeton professor Gerard O'Neill and $2,000 for Congresswoman Shirley Chisholm, plus expenses, with all the lectures free. Carwell added that tickets for the Heart concert at Diddle Arena on 15 February would go on sale on 22 January at $7 in advance and $8 on the day.
events.money: Gregory $4,000; O'Neill $2,000; Chisholm $2,000; Heart tickets $7 advance, $8 day of show

src.label: College Heights Herald, Vol. 54, No. 33, 18 January 1979

events.title: Heart at Diddle Arena
events.body: Heart played Diddle Arena on 15 February with Ann Wilson opening on "High Times" and her sister Nancy on guitar, running through "Heartless," "Straight On," "Magazine," "Mistral Wind," "Dog and Butterfly," "Hijinx," "Crazy on You" and "Barracuda." Sunshine Promotions had signed the band as its first major break for Western, but only 5,821 came, a little more than half of capacity. Western made about $5,200 from the show, the one clear financial success of the concert year.

events.title: Forum '79 cut to one night
events.body: ASG's gubernatorial candidates' discussion panel, scheduled for two nights, was shortened to one after the university orchestra needed Van Meter Auditorium on the Monday. President Steve Thornton said the surviving session would run at 7:30 p.m. on the Tuesday, with Democrats Carroll Hubbard, Ralph Ed Graves and George Atkins appearing and Lieutenant Governor Thelma Stovall sending a representative. Ray White was the only Republican candidate willing to attend; Terry McBrayer and Louie Nunn stayed away.

src.label: College Heights Herald, Vol. 54, No. 48, 27 March 1979

events.title: ASG's promoter had not signed a contract days before the Player and Exile concert
