events.body: ASG said in the early autumn of 1978 that it would sign a contract with Sunshine Promotions, an Indianapolis concert firm, and its activities vice president David Carwell said the company met the three requirements for an outside promoter: an office within 500 miles of Western, at least 75 major concerts promoted, and $2 million grossed on them. Eight days before the Player and Exile concert of 3 November, the Herald reported that Western had still not signed, because the firm would not post the $100,000 performance bond the university required to guarantee that all the bills would be paid. Sunshine's Sybesma said Indiana insurance companies wanted 100 per cent collateral and a $2,000 service fee for the bond, and said his company might instead put up money before each concert. Sunshine later posted an irrevocable letter of credit that Western could cash if the concert bills went unpaid.

src.label: College Heights Herald 54:19, 26 Oct 1978; 1979 Talisman, Associated Student Government section

events.title: Gerald O'Neill on space colonies
events.body: Gerald O'Neill, a physics professor at Princeton and author of "The High Frontier", told 100 people in the Center Theater in his lecture of 2 April 1979 that space colonies and solar power stations were possible with current technology, and that electricity from solar cells could be sent back to Earth as low energy microwaves. He said plans for space colonies existed but President Carter had abolished the NASA office exploring space colonisation, and that he was concerned about the militarisation of space because Carter had signed a bill to develop a particle beam weapon to be placed in space. The same yearbook records that lectures and concerts had been run by Associated Student Government until the Board of Regents voted on 31 March 1979 to hand that programming to a new University Center Board from the following autumn.

src.label: 1979 Talisman, Lectures p. 97 and University Center Board p. 81

events.title: Shirley Chisholm closed the Black Awareness Symposium
events.body: Congresswoman Shirley Chisholm cancelled her February lecture, which is why the former Black Awareness Week was stretched across the spring semester as a symposium, and her rescheduled talk on 18 April closed it. She spoke on America's unfulfilled legacies before a crowd of about 250, predominantly black, who shouted and chanted in response, describing herself as a people's politician who could not be manipulated and saying she was there to tell people what they did not want to hear. The same yearbook records that lectures and concerts had been run by Associated Student Government until a reorganised University Center Board took them over in the autumn of 1979.

src.label: Talisman 1979, Black Awareness Symposium and lectures sections

events.title: The Regents take concerts and lectures away from ASG
events.body: The Board of Regents approved a rebuilt University Center Board on 31 March 1979 and funded it with $80,000 for programming. From the autumn its committees of students and administrators would run the lectures and concerts Associated Student Government had been running. ASG kept three seats, held by its president, its activities vice president and one member of congress, alongside representatives of the Interfraternity and Panhellenic councils, United Black Students, the men's and women's residence hall councils, two other students and three faculty members. The university programs coordinator, Tim Nemeth, said the new board would involve more student participation, and then put its maximum at ten students working on lectures and concerts against the fifty involved under ASG.
events.money: $80,000 to the University Center Board for programming

leaders.name: James Hargroave
leaders.note: Surname spelling on the plaque is HARGROAVE. The Herald, in a 30 August 1979 profile calling him ASG Head at the start of the year, spells the name 'Jamie Hargrove.' Flagging the discrepancy rather than silently correcting the plaque spelling, per project rule.
profile: By August 30, 1979, at the start of the school year, the Herald profiled the Associated Student Government head - spelled 'Jamie Hargrove' in the byline - under the headline that he believed students were interested. The archive does not yet hold the spring 1979 election coverage that put him in office; see the events below for the primary that preceded it.

The archive does not yet show what Hargrove's administration passed or fought over during 1979-80 beyond the record's general sweep of the year. Further Herald issues from the fall and spring semester have not yet been checked.

events.title: 830 students vote in the ASG primary; the Herald runs a defence of not voting
events.body: The Associated Student Government's spring primary drew 830 voters and put the open-house policy on the ballot. The same issue carried a piece justifying student apathy in ASG voting - the paper had moved from scolding non-voters to explaining them. This primary elected the officers who took office for 1979-80; it was previously misfiled under 1978-79.

events.title: Donald Zacharias sworn in as WKU's sixth president
events.body: Zacharias, previously executive assistant to the chancellor of the University of Texas system, took office as WKU's sixth president at the opening of the academic year; he was formally installed the following spring.

events.title: ASG head Jamie Hargrove profiled at year's start
events.body: The Herald profiled the Associated Student Government head under the headline that he believed students were interested, in the same issue that introduced the new president's wife, Tommie Zacharias, to campus.

events.title: ASG weighs expanding hall representation
events.body: The Associated Student Government considered expanding residence hall representation in its congress, in the same issue reporting the Board of Regents set to consider a two-year budget request.

events.title: Resolution 79-10 seeks staff for scholarship administration
events.body: The Associated Student Government passed Resolution 79-10, urging the university to assign staff to administer academic scholarships.

events.title: Hargrove opens the year saying students are interested
events.body: Associated Student Government head Jamie Hargrove told the Herald he believed students were interested in their government as the year opened. A week later ASG heard its 1979-80 budget and discussed changing its delegate policy.

events.title: Seats bill passes after revision under pressure
events.body: A bill on Associated Student Government seats passed after being revised under pressure, expanding on earlier talk of broader residence hall representation. The Herald called the representation bill a small step in the right direction.

events.title: ASG rejects move to close Diddle Hall
events.body: The Associated Student Government rejected a move to close Diddle Hall dormitory. The vote came amid a fall of housing debates that later included a push to make Keen Hall a coed dorm.

events.title: ASG proposes an activity fee for part-time students
events.body: ASG proposed a part-time student activity fee. The proposal came as the Board of Regents weighed budget requests for the coming biennium.

events.title: ASG considers moving its spring elections
events.body: The Associated Student Government considered changing the date of its spring elections. The discussion took place against campus anger over a proposed tuition increase.

events.title: Fuller and Irons win the presidential primary
events.body: Steve Fuller and Tim Irons emerged as victors in the ASG presidential primary, from a field of three that also included David Rue. Candidates had been certified earlier in the month.

events.title: Steve Fuller elected ASG president
events.body: Steve Fuller, Mark Wilson and Greg Zoeller were elected to the top Associated Student Government jobs. The Herald wrote that persistence had paid off in Fuller's campaign, while runner-up Tim Irons looked to the future after losing.

events.title: New ASG officers and members sworn in
events.body: The new Associated Student Government officers and members were sworn in. ASG and the Interhall Council were also conducting student polls as the year closed.

events.title: ASG replaces concerts with opinion polls and a radio phone-in
events.body: Stripped of entertainment, ASG spent the year on student opinion polls, a phone-in programme on the campus station WKYU where President Jamie Hargrove answered questions, and expanded publicity for its own elections. Hargrove said the transfer of activities to the University Center Board had cost ASG between $60,000 and $70,000 of budget but no real power. Poll committee chairman Kevin Kinne said the university administration was showing a lot of support for the polls.
events.money: $60,000 to $70,000 of activities budget lost to the Center Board

events.title: ASG asks the bookstore to break even on books
events.body: ASG introduced a bill asking the College Heights Bookstore to adopt a break-even policy on book sales, arguing that the store had a monopoly on textbooks and that the College Heights Foundation which runs it is a non-profit organisation. Congress was to vote on it the following week. At the same meeting congress formed an ad hoc committee on university food services.

src.label: College Heights Herald, Vol. 55, No. 34, 31 January 1980

leaders.name: Steven Fuller
leaders.note: Herald bylines consistently call him "Steve Fuller"; the plaque and this site list "Steven Fuller" - spelling unverified.
profile: Steve Fuller entered the April 1980 Associated Student Government presidential race against David Rue and Tim Irons; the Herald covered ASG hopefuls debating the issues at an April 3 candidates' forum before reporting the three-way field on April 10.

Fuller won the presidency in the April 24 election, reported under the headline "Persistence Pays Off in Steve Fuller Campaign." Mark Wilson and Greg Zoeller were elected to other top ASG offices the same day; Tim Irons's loss was covered separately.

Fuller's fall term was consumed by a running fight over dormitory room inspections. A September 4 inspection measure was voted down amid criticism of how the vote was conducted; a September 11 bill calling for a ban on bugs in the dorms drew a mocking editorial cartoon and an editorial calling the university's protective inspection policy unnecessary; and by November 13 the Herald reported ASG had nearly slept through its own vote before re-endorsing inspections, followed a week later by a bill proposing a stricter room-entry rule.

In office, ASG under Fuller also proposed a change to the organization's own title in October 1980 and asked the state to evaluate higher education funding in February 1981, as budget worries dominated the legislative session. His successor, Marcel Bush, was elected that April.

Fuller entered the Associated Student Government presidential race in the spring of 1980 as one of three candidates. Michele Wood's Herald report was headlined "3 Running for Associated Student Government President," naming Steve Fuller, David Rue and Tim Irons.

During the 1980-81 year the Associated Student Government pressed the state on the condition of higher education, with Robert Pillow reporting in February 1981 that the body had asked the state to conduct an evaluation. The request came as the campus argued over budget cuts, including cuts to athletics.

events.title: ASG proposes a title change
events.body: The Associated Student Government proposed a title change for the organization. The proposal surfaced in the same week campus activities were limited for the national election day.

events.title: Sturgeon and Bush win the ASG primary
events.body: David Sturgeon and Marcel Bush won the Associated Student Government primary, in a campaign the Herald said saw candidates playing big time politics. The same issue carried a resolution asking for a new ASG logo.

events.title: Bush defeats Sturgeon for the presidency
events.body: David Sturgeon was defeated in the Associated Student Government race, leaving Marcel Bush the winner after endorsements had split between the two. The congress also voted to keep the present ASG logo.

events.title: Close races prompt ASG recounts
events.body: Close races prompted recounts in the Associated Student Government election. The recounts came in the same week the Council on Higher Education approved a tuition increase.

events.title: ASG changes its mind on changing minds
events.body: The Herald reported that the Associated Student Government changed its mind on changing minds, capping a contentious election month. The same issue covered a withdrawn regent selection and the board's study of reorganizing the university.

events.title: Three seek the ASG presidency
events.body: Steve Fuller, David Rue and Tim Irons entered the race for Associated Student Government president.

events.title: Fuller elected ASG president
events.body: Steve Fuller won the Associated Student Government presidency over David Rue and Tim Irons. Mark Wilson and Greg Zoeller were elected to other top ASG offices the same day.

events.title: ASG hopefuls debate the issues; ASG weighs opposing a UCB change
events.body: Associated Student Government presidential hopefuls discussed the issues and courted votes at a candidates' forum ahead of the spring election. The same issue reported ASG considering opposition to a proposed change to the University Center Board's structure.

events.title: ASG room inspection measure defeated amid criticism
events.body: A proposed ASG measure on dormitory room inspections was voted down, in a session a separate Herald article criticized for how the vote was conducted. The defeat opened a fall-long fight over dorm inspection policy.

events.title: ASG bill targets pests in the dorms
events.body: ASG introduced a bill calling for a ban on bugs in residence halls; the Herald's editorial cartoon depicted a cockroach imperiled by the resolution. The paper's editorial page separately argued the university's protective inspection policy was unnecessary.

events.title: ASG re-endorses dorm inspections after nearly missing the vote
events.body: ASG voted to re-endorse dormitory room inspections, in a session the Herald reported the government had nearly slept through. The same issue covered ASG's sponsorship of an international film and dance series and an attorney's interest in a dorm inspection case.

events.title: ASG bill proposes a stricter room-entry rule
events.body: ASG introduced a bill proposing a stricter rule governing staff entry into student rooms, continuing the fall's running fight over dormitory inspections.

events.title: Resolution 80-32 asks for change machines in the dorms
events.body: ASG passed Resolution 80-32, requesting that change machines be installed in residence halls.

events.title: International Food Fest and fashion show
events.body: In the spring semester ASG followed International Week with an International Food Fest and fashion show. International students committee chairman Osama Shariff, a junior from Jerusalem, said attendance at the autumn programmes had been very good and that they were well put together. The Talisman called International Week the highlight of ASG's autumn semester.

events.title: ASG's car pool match-up
events.body: ASG ran a car pool match-up scheme jointly with the Barren River Area Development District and hoped to continue it. Almost 450 students took part across the two semesters. It was one of the few concrete services the organisation carried through in a year the Talisman headlined as a year of resolutions.

events.title: ASG's International Week
events.body: Associated Student Government sponsored International Week, which ran nightly from Monday 10 November 1980 and closed with a presentation on Brazil and Colombia on the Thursday evening. Two or three countries were featured each night through films, lectures, folk dances and slides given by students and faculty from those countries, and programme chairman Osama Shariff opened the week with a talk on Palestine and a Red Cross film on Palestinian children. The 1981 Talisman, which spells him Sharif and calls him international students committee chairman, credits the week to student government and the International Students Committee, places the nightly programmes in the university center, and lists nine countries: Switzerland, Palestine, Iceland, Malaysia, Colombia, Brazil, India, Pakistan and France.

events.title: ASG asked the state to evaluate higher education
events.body: The Associated Student Government called on the state to carry out an evaluation of higher education. Robert Pillow reported the request in the Herald of 5 February 1981, an issue dominated by budget pressure across Kentucky's universities and by controversy over cuts to the athletic budget.

organization.note: Mark Wilson and Greg Zoeller were elected to other top ASG offices in the same April 1980 election; the Herald index does not specify which.

leaders.name: Marcell Bush
leaders.note: Herald bylines consistently spell this "Marcel Bush" (one L); the plaque and this site list "Marcell Bush" - spelling unverified. Resigned the ASG presidency 14 January 1982; David Payne succeeded him for the balance of the term.
profile: Marcel Bush won the Associated Student Government presidency in April 1981, defeating David Sturgeon after a campaign the Herald said saw candidates "playing big time politics." Close races elsewhere on the ballot prompted recounts.

In office that fall, ASG raised its own campaign spending limit and vetoed a plan to pay an education lobbyist, days after rallying publicly for higher education funding. Bush later listed the fall rally as one achievement of his term.

Bush resigned the presidency on or shortly before 14 January 1982, reported the same week as the retrospective on his term. David Payne succeeded him; Board of Regents minutes from 30 January 1982 name Payne the new SGA president.

leaders.name: David Payne
leaders.note: Plaque reads 1982; this site originally filed him under 1982-83. Board of Regents minutes (30 Jan 1982) and Herald coverage place him as SGA president succeeding Marcel Bush, who resigned 14 Jan 1982, filling the balance of the 1981-82 term. Margaret Ragan, elected president in April 1982, led the separate 1982-83 term - the two are not the same office-year. The Herald of 14 January 1982 photographed Payne, then Associated Student Government vice president, announcing the resignation of president and student regent Marcell Bush, whom he succeeded.

sources.label: WKU Board of Regents minutes, 30 Jan 1982

profile: David Payne first appears in the indexed record in February 1981 with a Herald letter titled 'Apathy Erased.' By October 1981, before he held the presidency, he was writing on the Associated Student Government's behalf, declaring that ASG was rallying for higher education as budget cuts loomed.

Payne became ASG's president after Marcel Bush resigned on 14 January 1982; Board of Regents minutes from the January 30 meeting name him the new SGA president. In early February the Herald reported that Payne wanted another adviser for ASG, and its editorial page attacked his judgment, while a report the next week said Payne considered certain resolutions misdirected.

Later that month, letter writers to the Herald argued that Payne had been made a victim in the affair; the indexed headline does not state what precipitated it. His name does not appear in the indexed headlines of the April 1982 election that chose Margaret Ragan for the 1982-83 term, nor in the 1982-83 issues examined - consistent with his presidency ending with Bush's original term.

events.title: Sandra Norfleet elected student regent
events.body: Reported by Kevin Francke. The same issue has a group set to speak on the Associated Student Government's behalf and Western's 1982 budget coming off hold.

events.title: ASG announces its goals for the year
events.body: The Associated Student Government announced its goals for the coming year. Within two weeks its executives were defending their actions in the Herald, whose editorial page complained that petty politics plagued the organization.

events.title: Campaign spending limit raised
events.body: ASG voted to increase its campaign spending limit. The change followed a week of debate over whether the cap should rise.

events.title: ASG vetoes plan to pay an education lobbyist
events.body: The Associated Student Government vetoed a plan to pay an education lobbyist. The vote came weeks after ASG had rallied publicly for higher education funding.

events.title: Five students seek the student regent seat
events.body: Five students sought the student regent spot in the first campus-wide election for the seat. The February 9 vote produced no majority, forcing a runoff the following week.

events.title: Ragan and Sargent survive the presidential primary
events.body: Margaret Ragan and Glenn Sargent survived the Associated Student Government presidential primary. The field had included Jack Smith, Kerrie Stewart and Jack Murphree, whose supporters filled the Herald's letters pages.

events.title: General election results voided
events.body: The student government election results were voided, a decision the Herald said disgusted the candidates. A repeat general election was scheduled for April 20.

events.title: Margaret Ragan wins the repeated election
events.body: Margaret Ragan won the ASG presidency in the repeated general election. The new officers were sworn in the following week.

events.title: ASG president Marcel Bush resigns
events.body: Associated Student Government president Marcel Bush resigned. The same issue reported him listing the fall's higher-education rally as one achievement of his term.

events.title: Board of Regents minutes name David Payne the new SGA president
events.body: Minutes of the WKU Board of Regents meeting identified David Payne as the new Student Government Association president, confirming his succession after Marcel Bush's resignation.

events.title: Payne asks for a second ASG adviser
events.body: President David Payne said the Associated Student Government wanted another adviser. The Herald's editorial page criticized his judgment the same week.

events.title: Norfleet's short regent term nears its end
events.body: The Herald noted that the student regent's two-month term was already nearing its end, a reminder of how short a stopgap the office had been.

events.title: ASG and the University Center Board both ask for more money
events.body: The Herald reported that the Associated Student Government and the University Center Board both wanted larger budgets and planned to submit requests. Two weeks later the paper ran a piece arguing that the Center Board outshone ASG.

events.title: The discount cards that never existed
events.body: ASG announced it would file complaints with the Better Business Bureaus of Georgia and Texas against University Press Inc. of Lewisville, Texas, and Atlanta, which had taken $275 from each of at least four Bowling Green merchants for ASG-endorsed student discount cards that were never produced. A man calling himself Louis F. Cordoba had told Gary Smith of the Bouquet Shoppe on the U.S. 31-W By-Pass that then-president Steve Fuller had recommended his shop as an advertiser, and Smith wrote a $275 cheque on 18 March. The cards were supposed to have been handed out at registration for the autumn.
events.money: $275 taken from each of at least four merchants

src.label: College Heights Herald, Vol. 57, No. 5, 10 September 1981

events.title: 14,000 cards, a dead phone line and a returned letter
events.body: President Marcel Bush had spent three weeks trying to reach the company printing 14,000 ASG discount cards: the Texas number was disconnected, an answering service pushed her to an Atlanta number nobody answered, and a letter to the Texas address came back from the post office. On the day complaints were being filed, company representative Phil Bewley finally telephoned to say the cards had shipped from New York and that printing problems had caused the delay. The Herald noted that until two years earlier ASG had printed discount cards at its own expense as a free student service, charging merchants nothing, and had dropped it when costs became prohibitive.
events.money: 14,000 cards; merchants paid $275 for a listing

src.label: College Heights Herald, Vol. 57, No. 10, 29 September 1981

events.title: Discount cards arrive, but do not go out
events.body: The ASG discount cards reached campus the day before the Herald's report of 1 October 1981. There were 14,000 of them and they offered students discounts at 21 listed merchants, valid until 1 September 1982. They were not handed out: Bush had been busy with other projects and passed the job to the communications committee, whose chairwoman, Laura Simms, was still working on a plan.

events.title: ASG appointed a council to settle its internal disputes
events.body: The Associated Student Government appointed a council to decide disputes inside the organization. The Herald report, by Kevin Francke, ran two weeks after his coverage of the resignation of ASG president Marcel Bush. The same issue reported that the regents bill, changing how the student regent was chosen, had passed the state House.

leaders.name: Sandra Norfleet
leaders.note: Student regent, not president. Election reported in the Herald, 18 February 1982.
profile: No candidate won a majority on February 9, forcing a runoff, which Norfleet won on February 16. The Herald reported her election as student regent in its February 18 issue.

Her initial term was short: by mid-April 1982 the Herald noted that the student regent's 2-month term was nearing its end. She is listed among the 1982-83 student leaders, and in February 1983 the Herald's editorial page was still weighing the office, insisting the student regent must represent everyone.

Norfleet reached the student regent seat through a crowded contest. The Herald reported on 2 February 1982 that five students were seeking the student regent spot, and two days later Kevin Francke ran a piece in which the candidates set out their qualities.

Kevin Francke reported on 18 February 1982 that Sandra Norfleet had been elected student regent. The same issue carried his story on a group that would speak on the Associated Student Government's behalf.

Her time in the seat was short. By mid-April Francke was reporting that the student regent's two-month term was nearing its end, in an issue that also covered voided ASG election results and a joke resolution that nearly passed the congress.

leaders.name: Margaret Ragan
leaders.note: Confirmed by her own byline in the Herald, 3 Feb 1983 ('Ragan, Margaret. Associated Student Government, Student Regent Position Separate'), plus the primary and election-night headlines in the same spring.
profile: Margaret Ragan survived the April 1982 Associated Student Government presidential primary along with Glenn Sargent, emerging from a five-way field. Endorsement letters for her ran in the Herald through both rounds of the election.
After the first general election was voided, Ragan won the presidency in the repeated election held April 20, 1982. She and the other new officers were sworn in before the month was out.

Midway through her term Ragan used the Herald's pages to explain that the ASG presidency and the student regent seat were now separate positions. Her spring saw a grade plan, a student shuttle vote, and a contested rewrite of the ASG constitution before Jack Smith was elected to succeed her.

Ragan's presidency came out of a disrupted spring. The Associated Student Government repeated its general election on 20 April 1982, after the Herald had reported the previous week that the first round's results were void.

She set out her agenda at the start of the fall term. Monica Dias reported in the Herald's second issue of the year that major ASG changes were envisioned by Margaret Ragan, and over the following months the congress took up a campus Wall of Fame, a joint coed housing poll with the Interhall Council, and a coed housing bill it approved in November.

Ragan also argued in print for keeping the two student offices distinct. In February 1983 the Herald carried her statement that the Associated Student Government and the student regent position were separate, in the same issue that reported the ASG shuttle service.

events.title: Norfleet wins the student regent runoff
events.body: No candidate won a majority in the February 9 student regent primary, forcing a runoff. Sandra Norfleet won the runoff on February 16.

events.title: Ragan and Sargent survive the ASG primary
events.body: Margaret Ragan and Glenn Sargent survived the Associated Student Government presidential primary, emerging from a five-way field.

events.title: Ragan wins the presidency in a repeated election
events.body: The first general election was voided, and Margaret Ragan won the Associated Student Government presidency in the repeated election held April 20. She and the other new officers were sworn in before the month was out.

events.title: ASG floats a shuttle service, and Ragan explains the split with the regent seat
events.body: The same issue that carried President Margaret Ragan's Herald piece explaining that the ASG presidency and student regent seat were now separate positions also reported ASG was considering a shuttle service, the proposal put to a student vote the following week.

events.title: Grade plan passes; students vote for a shuttle
events.body: ASG passed a grade plan, and 206 students voted for a campus shuttle service.

events.title: Constitution changes approved; filing opens
events.body: The Associated Student Government approved changes to its constitution, and ten students filed for offices ahead of the deadline. Dean Charles Keown publicly questioned the revisions the following week, as filings swelled to 68.

events.title: 500 vote in the ASG primary
events.body: About 500 students voted in the Associated Student Government primary. The Herald's letters pages carried a steady stream of endorsements for presidential candidate Jack Smith.

events.title: Jack Smith wins the ASG presidency
events.body: Jack Smith won the presidency of the Associated Student Government, and students voted for the ASG constitutional revisions on the same ballot. The Herald had dared students to vote at all in a sardonic election day editorial.

events.title: 24 elected to Senate
events.body: Twenty-four students were elected to the Associated Student Government Senate, the same issue reporting increased dormitory hours had been proposed.

events.title: ASG endorses a $15 athletic fee
events.body: The outgoing congress endorsed a $15 athletic fee. The vote came as the Board of Regents turned its focus to the budget.

events.title: ASG endorses William Natcher
events.body: The Herald reported that the Associated Student Government had backed William Natcher. The same issue previewed the ASG presidential primary set for the following Tuesday, and five days later the paper editorialized that endorsing was not wise for ASG.

events.title: Ragan opens the year promising major ASG changes
events.body: Monica Dias reported that major ASG changes were envisioned by Margaret Ragan. The story ran in the Herald's second issue of the fall semester and was the paper's first substantial account of her plans.

events.title: ASG considers a Wall of Fame
events.body: Monica Dias reported that the Associated Student Government was considering a Wall of Fame. A week later the Herald followed with a report that the wall looked promising.

events.title: ASG approves a coed housing bill
events.body: Monica Dias reported that the Associated Student Government had approved a coed housing bill. The measure built through the fall: ASG and the Interhall Council polled students on coed housing in September, and ASG formally proposed it on 10 November.

events.title: ASG breaks from the student legislature
events.body: Monica Dias reported that the Associated Student Government had broken from the student legislature. The break did not last, and by February 1984 the Herald was reporting that the Kentucky Intercollegiate State Legislature might join ASG again.

events.title: No quorum, so ASG does not meet
events.body: The Herald reported that the Associated Student Government failed to reach a quorum and did not meet. It was the first ASG item the paper carried after the winter break.

events.title: A volunteer student escort service
events.body: A student escort service jointly sponsored by Interhall Council, ASG and the university police began operating, walking women anywhere on campus from dark until midnight Sunday to Thursday on a single telephone number, with a vehicle in bad weather. Coordinator James Hunter said Western was the first university in the country with a completely volunteer, student-operated escort service, and that it had filled about 500 to 600 requests in its first year without a single incident. Public safety director Paul Bunch said requests for escorts had tripled after two students were raped the previous year.
events.money: 500 to 600 requests filled in the first year

executive.note: Separately elected office; her term ran only from mid-February to roughly mid-April 1982, a two-month stopgap before the 1982-83 cycle.

leaders.name: Jack Smith
leaders.note: Two-year plate. Confirmed by name in Herald headlines across his whole term, from the April 1983 win through the April 1985 retrospective on his presidency ending.
profile: Jack Smith first ran for the Associated Student Government presidency in spring 1982, drawing repeated endorsement letters in the Herald, and though Margaret Ragan won that race, Smith and Lonnie Sears took awards as the year closed. He returned as a candidate in March 1983, when 68 students filed for ASG positions and his supporters again filled the letters pages.

Smith won the presidency of the Associated Student Government in the April 12, 1983 election, in which students also approved constitutional revisions. His victory came after roughly 500 students had voted in the primary the week before.

His presidency was colorful and contentious: the fall brought a discount card controversy, letters accusing him of partying while committees waited and others defending him, and a December cartoon that he wrote in to protest. In April 1984 the Herald caught him impersonating a bunny as his ASG ran a low-turnout poll on beer and a campus pub.

Smith's plaque term runs two years, 1983-85, and the Herald's own account of his exit backs that up: its April 11, 1985 issue reported him ending his term as ASG president in an article headlined 'Jack Smith Ends Term as Associated Student Government President,' alongside a companion piece crediting his enthusiasm with reviving interest in the organization.

Smith's 1983 campaign drew an unusual run of supporting letters in the Herald. The issue of 7 April 1983 carried two, from Dorothy Metzmeler and Sarah Hein, following one from Tony Johnson the week before; the same issue reported that about 500 students had voted in the ASG primary.

Jamie Morton reported on 14 April 1983 that Jack Smith had won the presidency of the Associated Student Government. The same issue reported that students had also voted in favor of the ASG constitutional revisions worked out that spring.

His first term drew heavy comment. In December 1983 the Herald reported that ASG had voided its own procedures even as it saw growth in membership and took up fourteen proposals, and the same issue carried Stanley Reagan's letter headed "Jack Smith, Associated Student Government Thrown Away" along with another Lou Bloss cartoon on ASG. He filed for re-election in February 1984 and stayed in office through a second year, ending his term in April 1985.

events.title: Escort service returns; discount card floated
events.body: The Herald's opening issue reported that the student escort service would resume and that ASG might sponsor a discount card. Filing for freshman elections was set to begin September 19.

events.title: Discount card plan draws fire
events.body: ASG voted to study the discount card after the Herald editorialized that the organization should govern, not market cards. A week later the paper reported ASG would offer members a commission on card sales, prompting letters calling the plan cheap shots and old tricks.

events.title: ASG passes incomplete-grade deadline proposal
events.body: The Associated Student Government passed its proposal on the deadline for incomplete grades, after tabling it the week before. The grade issue had occupied ASG since September.

events.title: ASG voids its own procedures amid growth
events.body: The Herald reported that ASG voided its own procedures, while also noting growth in membership and a congress weighing 14 proposals. The editorial page mocked the body with a cartoon, and Jack Smith wrote in to say the cartoon aggravated him.

events.title: Student legislature may rejoin ASG
events.body: The Kentucky Student Legislature delegation was reported possibly rejoining the Associated Student Government. Letter writers sparred the same day over whether the ASG stereotype was deserved.

events.title: Top four ASG offices decided without runoffs
events.body: The top four Associated Student Government spots were decided, the Herald reported, as ASG emphasized representation. About 450 students had voted in the primary the week before.

events.title: ASG polls students on beer and a campus pub
events.body: ASG began a student poll on the beer and campus pub issue on general election day. The Herald's editorial page argued the economics of the campus pub plan were faulty.

events.title: Low turnout may force a beer poll revote
events.body: Low turnout threatened to spur a revote in the ASG beer poll. The same issue reported president Jack Smith impersonating a bunny for the season.

events.title: ASG election day: candidates court votes for the top offices
events.body: The Herald urged students to the polls for the Associated Student Government election. Beyond the presidential contest, candidates for ASG's other top offices - including Bob Shults, Laura McClellan, Traci Turner, Kim Binkley and Allan Kujala - each drew endorsement letters in the paper; the Herald index does not specify which office each sought.

events.title: Smith opens with a "year of action"
events.body: Steve Paul reported that the Associated Student Government was planning for a year of action. The story ran in the third issue of the fall semester, a week after the Herald first reported that ASG might sponsor a discount card.

events.title: ASG members to take a commission on discount cards
events.body: Steve Paul reported that the Associated Student Government would offer its members a commission on the discount cards. The same issue carried two critical columns aimed at ASG, Timi Flener's "Cheap Shots" and Connie Hoffman's "And Old Tricks."

events.title: ASG asks for cable television in dorm rooms
events.body: Steve Paul reported that the Associated Student Government wanted cable in dormitory rooms. The same issue ran a Lou Bloss editorial cartoon on an ASG penalty and a letter from Carl Davis disagreeing with an ASG proposal.

events.title: Budget falls short as the grade plan passes
events.body: Craig Dezern and Steve Paul reported that the ASG budget would not cover its planned projects. The same issue reported that ASG had approved its grade plan, the change to the grading scale that ran through most of the year.

events.title: ASG takes up a university day-care center
events.body: Barry Rose reported that a university day-care center would be studied by the Associated Student Government. It joined study hall research and cable television among the service questions ASG picked up that fall.

events.title: Vice president William Chandler quits
events.body: Victoria Malmer reported that Associated Student Government vice president William Chandler had quit. Within a week the Herald reported that three people had been nominated for ASG positions.

events.title: The top ASG officers file for re-election
events.body: Mark Edelen reported that the top Associated Student Government officers were seeking re-election. The same issue reported that legislators were upset with ASG and that students were being asked to gripe, and it carried further responses to the alcohol poll plan.

events.title: ASG prints the discount card itself
events.body: After an agreement collapsed with University Services Associates of St. Mary's, Missouri, ASG voted to print the student discount cards itself, and they were finally handed out in November through the Student Affairs and Public Relations committees working with Interhall Council. Nine businesses appeared on the card, among them the seven merchants who had paid company president George Wheaton for the original card and never got a refund. President Jack Smith said the businesses would have to recover their own money: "They got what they paid for. They got their discount card."
events.money: nine businesses on the card; seven merchants unrefunded

src.label: College Heights Herald, Vol. 59, No. 23, 10 November 1983

organization.note: Bob Shults, Laura McClellan, Traci Turner, Kim Binkley and Allan Kujala all appear as candidates for ASG's top offices in the April 1983 election coverage; the Herald index does not specify which offices they sought or who won them.

leaders.name: Jack Smith
leaders.note: Two-year plate. Either re-elected or the plaque compresses two terms. Confirmed from inside the term: the Herald of 20 March 1984 reported the top four ASG posts decided, and coverage through 1984-85 names Smith as president in his second year.
profile: Smith presided over a productive opening to the 1984-85 year. By the third week of September the Herald reported that four ASG proposals had been made reality, and the congress had begun studying a student book exchange, which became the signature project of his final year.
By mid-year the record was mixed. The book exchange venture appeared likely to take a summer pause, and the organization was weighing whether to fight cuts to education funding.

His term ended in April 1985. The Herald covered his exit with a news story headlined that Smith was ending his term as ASG president, an editorial crediting his enthusiasm with reviving interest in the organization, and an editorial cartoon. The SGA plaque records him on a two-year 1983-85 plate.

Jack Smith first won the presidency of the Associated Student Government in a race the College Heights Herald reported under the headline "Jack Smith Wins Presidency of Associated Student Government," in the paper's fifty-eighth volume. That win put him in the office he would go on to hold across more than one term.

Smith and the Herald did not always get along. One issue in the paper's fifty-ninth volume indexed an item headed "Jack Smith, Associated Student Government Thrown Away" together with a letter written by Smith himself under the title "Cartoon Aggravates," showing that he answered the paper's cartoonists in print rather than letting the criticism stand.

His time in office closed in April 1985, when Mack Humphreys wrote up Smith ending his term as Associated Student Government president. The Herald ran a second piece in the same issue crediting Smith's enthusiasm with reviving interest in ASG, and Kevin Knapp marked the departure with an editorial cartoon on Smith and the organisation.

events.title: Apathy as an editorial cartoon
events.body: 'Voter Apathy Can be Solved' ran alongside a cartoon on election apathy and a report that a 24-hour open house was under discussion.

events.title: Four proposals made reality in the third week of class
events.body: The Herald reported that four Associated Student Government proposals had already been carried out, and that the congress was beginning a study of a student book exchange. The exchange went on to become the running project of the year.

events.title: The grade scale proposal is denied
events.body: ASG's proposal for a new grade scale was denied, one week after the congress's early run of successes. It was the first setback of the fall reported in the Herald's coverage.

events.title: ASG wants less general education
events.body: The congress went on record wanting a reduction in general education requirements. It was an early instance of the body intervening in curriculum policy, three years before the fights over the General Education Task Force.

events.title: LaMont Jones drops out of a revote
events.body: LaMont Jones withdrew from an ASG revote, and the same issue carried an editorial cartoon on the organization. A disputed election requiring a revote marked the low point of the fall semester.

events.title: Education cuts loom and the book exchange stalls
events.body: ASG weighed a fight against state education cuts, while its book exchange venture looked likely to pause for the summer. Both stories ran in the same late-January issue.

events.title: Four file for congress president
events.body: A fourth candidate filed for ASG congress president and a debate was set, as the spring filing period opened. The same issue carried letters both applauding an ASG bill and requesting its support.

events.title: McKinney and Watkins take the primary
events.body: Mitchell McKinney and Chris Watkins rode their experience to victory in the ASG primary. The congress also passed a resolution on grade point averages the same week.

events.title: ASG candidates debated ahead of the spring election
events.body: Mack Humphreys covered a debate in which Associated Student Government candidates aired their views before the spring vote. The same issue of the Herald carried student letters backing Greg Elder, Chris Watkins and Mitchell McKinney, showing that the race to succeed Jack Smith was contested.

events.title: A reader disputed the Herald's editorial on ASG
events.body: The Herald printed a letter from Luis Dickson taking issue with an editorial the paper had run about Associated Student Government. The letter appeared in the middle of the spring campaign season.

events.title: An apathy editorial greets a 24-hour open house debate
events.body: The Herald ran an apathy editorial and cartoon aimed at student government alongside a report on debate over 24-hour open house policy in the dorms.

events.title: Dueling op-eds spar over forcing a bill
events.body: The Herald ran a pair of opposing opinion pieces, both headlined "Associated Student Government Shouldn't Force Bill," one by future ASG president Mitchell McKinney and the other by Jamie Morton.

events.title: ASG votes to study a book exchange
events.body: ASG voted to study the feasibility of a student book exchange and formed a committee to examine schemes at the universities of Louisville and Kentucky. Two models were discussed: a room where students sold and bought books at prices they set, and a cheaper list of students, telephone numbers, books for sale and asking prices. President Jack Smith said books were more expensive every year and students needed somewhere besides the College Heights Bookstore, adding, "I don't think there's anything wrong with a little competition."

src.label: College Heights Herald, Vol. 60, No. 7, 20 September 1984

events.title: Book exchange ambassadors work the campus
events.body: ASG sent "ambassadors" out to campus organisations to explain the new book exchange and hand out registration cards, with public relations vice president John Holland promising to send a speaker "faster than Domino's pizza." Registration cards went into campus mailboxes on 5 December and had to be returned by 21 December, with an off-campus coupon printed in the Herald. The list of available books was to be compiled over Christmas and published as a tabloid of names, telephone numbers and titles when students returned in January.

src.label: College Heights Herald, Vol. 60, No. 24, 29 November 1984

events.title: The book exchanger's first edition
events.body: The tabloid book exchanger was distributed in the first week of the spring semester and students began telephoning each other to haggle over used textbooks. Committee co-chairmen John Holland and senior class president Danny Broderick, with President Jack Smith and administrative secretary Debra Stahl, keyed the entries into an IBM Personal Computer over the Christmas break on a program written for $25 by Bill Chestnut, a computer science graduate from Berea; Ginger Williams of the Franklin Favorite did the typesetting. Smith said the University of Kentucky had listed 700 books in its first exchange and Western had double that, and Broderick said ASG made no money from it: "This was a labor of love."
events.money: $25 paid for the computer program; about 1,400 books listed

events.title: ASG takes Big Brothers/Big Sisters children to a Lady Toppers game
events.body: Congress members each paired themselves with a child from Big Brothers/Big Sisters of Bowling Green for the women's last home basketball game, spending the evening counting heads, running trips to the bathroom and making enough noise to see the Lady Toppers past Cincinnati 122-72. Before the game the children ate snacks, made banners for the spirit contest and played pool and video games in the university center. The Herald reported that mothers in the crowd gave the student government members understanding looks.

src.label: College Heights Herald, Vol. 60, No. 43, 5 March 1985

events.title: Jack Smith ended his term as ASG president
events.body: The Herald of 11 April 1985 marked the end of Jack Smith's term as Associated Student Government president with a news story by Mack Humphreys. A companion editorial credited Smith's enthusiasm with reviving student interest in ASG, and Kevin Knapp drew an editorial cartoon on Smith and the organisation. Mitchell McKinney had been elected the new president the week before.

leaders.name: Mitchell McKinney
leaders.note: Named explicitly as SGA president in the outgoing congress's own commendation bill, Bill 86-13-S (3 Apr 1986), which settles the name.

sources.label: SGA Bill 86-13-S, Commendation of President, 3 Apr 1986

profile: Before he was a candidate, McKinney wrote a Herald op-ed on 21 March 1985 headlined 'Associated Student Government Shouldn't Force Bill,' one of a pair of dueling pieces the paper ran on the same question - a sign he was already active in ASG's legislative debates a week before he entered the presidential race.

McKinney won the spring 1985 primary on a ticket with Chris Watkins on March 28, the Herald's headline saying the pair rode experience to their primary victory over a field that included candidate Stan Reagan. He was announced as the new Associated Student Government president in the Herald of April 4, in the same issue that reported an unnamed legislative group rejoining ASG. The record found so far does not confirm what office, if any, Watkins went on to hold.

In office, the congress abolished its own Finance Committee that September and, the following spring, wrote a Financial Advisory Council into the ASG bylaws in its place. The spring 1986 session was especially active: bills created major/minor college representative seats, revised the membership application process, asked Board of Regents members to attend an SGA meeting, sought chains for Pearce-Ford Tower windows, and pushed for a welcome sign at Normal Drive and University Boulevard.

In March 1986 McKinney pulled out of the race for a second term. The same issue carried a piece arguing that student government needed a strong leader, and the field he left behind grew to four candidates before Tim Todd won the presidency that April. The outgoing congress commended McKinney's work in Bill 86-13-S on April 3, and the WKU Board of Regents included a resolution honoring him, alongside outgoing president John D. Minton, at its meeting of August 8, 1986. A 1986 presidential proclamation he signed honoring English professor Thomas Jones survives in the SGA records.

events.title: A 20-vote margin and a GPA debate
events.body: About 20 votes separated the top two finishers in a fall ASG election, and the congress debated setting a grade-point average requirement for its own members. Both stories ran in the same late-October issue.

events.title: Alcohol on campus studied again
events.body: ASG returned to the question of alcohol on campus, an issue that had already produced a student poll and a campus pub debate in 1984. The congress opened a new study of the policy.

events.title: A shuttle to the mall
events.body: The congress discussed running a shuttle service from campus to the mall. It was one of several consumer-service ideas, alongside student discount cards, floated that fall.

events.title: Lighting proposal defeated
events.body: Student government defeated a campus lighting proposal in the last week of the fall semester. It was one of the few outright defeats of legislation reported that year.

events.title: Fall-break bill narrowly passes
events.body: A bill calling for a fall break narrowly passed ASG. The proposal drew an opposing editorial in the next issue calling the extra break impractical and not needed.

events.title: No day off for Martin Luther King Day
events.body: ASG rejected a proposal to dismiss classes for the Martin Luther King holiday, one week after passing the fall-break bill. The King holiday question returned to the congress the following year.

events.title: McKinney withdraws from re-election
events.body: Mitchell McKinney pulled out of the race for a second term as ASG president. The same issue carried a piece arguing that student government needed a strong leader.

events.title: Library hours proposals, and elections delayed a week
events.body: ASG proposals asked for more library hours, and the spring elections were pushed back a week. The same issue carried dueling letters on whether the organization was in trouble.

events.body: The congress adopted a revised application process for SGA membership.

events.body: The congress asked for chains to be placed on Pearce-Ford Tower windows so they could be opened.

events.body: The outgoing congress passed a bill commending the work of SGA president Mitchell McKinney as his term ended.
